Travemünde heute is an independent, privately run information service by Christian Fizia, who lives in Travemünde. The site launched on 1 July 2026 and has been expanded and edited continuously since. It is not an official site of the Hanseatic City of Lübeck, the resort administration or Lübeck und Travemünde Marketing GmbH – and does not present itself as one. Full operator details under § 5 DDG (German Digital Services Act) are in the imprint; questions, corrections and tips are welcome via the contact page.

At its core is day-to-day information about the Baltic seaside resort of Travemünde: events with date, venue and source; water temperature, water level and the official bathing-water rating; live departures of trains, buses and the Priwall ferry; parking, getting here and Travemünde Week. Editorial topic pages – from beach chairs and fish rolls to the Brodten cliff – and a directory of restaurants, playgrounds and sights complete the picture. All content is available in German and English. AI agents and other programs can request the homepage as Markdown (Accept: text/markdown) and find an overview at /llms.txt.

Every number carries its source and a timestamp. Live readings come from open, named sources: weather and water temperature from Open-Meteo, the water level from the official Pegelonline gauge service (WSV), the bathing-water rating from Schleswig-Holstein open data, place data from OpenStreetMap, events from editorial curation and the openly licensed dataset of the Schleswig-Holstein tourism agency. What the site does not know for certain, it does not claim – overdue entries are visibly marked rather than hidden. The site shows no advertising and no paid placements. Places and events are not listed or favoured in exchange for money. The methodology page explains how each section works in detail.

Travemünde heute is a static website: data is fetched on the build server when the site is generated, the site is rebuilt several times a day and delivered as finished pages. Visiting it triggers no requests from your browser to data sources; there are no cookies, no personal tracking and therefore no consent banner. External maps load only after an explicit click. Travemünde is a Baltic seaside resort and, since 1913, the north-easternmost district of the Hanseatic city of Lübeck, where the Trave meets the Bay of Lübeck – about 15 kilometres from central Lübeck. Around 13,900 people live across 41.31 km². This page gathers the key figures, landmarks and facts – each with a source and verification date. 1187 year founded 13,903 inhabitants (2024) 41.31 square kilometres 1539 Germany’s oldest lighthouse ≈ 4 km of Baltic bathing shore 1 M+ visitors per year

Travemünde lies where the Trave meets the Bay of Lübeck: the town centre with the Vorderreihe on the west bank, the roughly three-kilometre Priwall peninsula on the east bank, linked by the Priwall ferry. Besides Alt-Travemünde and the Priwall, the district includes the three villages of Brodten, Teutendorf and Ivendorf, incorporated in 1935. North of the Kurstrand runs the Brodten cliff coast – an active cliff up to 20 metres high over about four kilometres towards Niendorf, popular for walks. Two official bathing waters are classified “excellent” under the EU directive; the bathing shore totals about four kilometres (promenade beach approx. 1 km, Priwall approx. 1.2 km). The Bay of Lübeck is part of the Baltic Sea – how the Baltic and the North Sea differ has its own page.

Skandinavienkai is Germany’s most important Baltic ferry port. Ferries run from here to Sweden (Trelleborg, Malmö, Karlshamn), Finland and the Baltics; through traffic bypasses the town via a dedicated junction to the B75. Tourism counts over a million overnight and day visitors a year; around 20 cruise ships dock annually at the Ostpreußenkai on the Vorderreihe. Trains stop at three stations (Skandinavienkai, Hafen, Strand); the line from Lübeck has been electrified since 2008 and runs hourly. By car the A1 and the B75 (the “Bäderstraße”) lead here; the Priwall ferry links the town centre with the Priwall peninsula year-round.

Travemünde was recognised as a seaside resort in 1802 – the second on the German Baltic coast. In season the beaches hold up to 1,500 beach chairs. Its best-known event is Travemünde Week, held since 1889, which with around 2,500 competitors and over 1,000 boats ranks among the largest sailing events in the world. Add the sand sculpture exhibition at the fishing harbour and a Christmas market at the cruise terminal. From 1949 to 2012 the town also had a casino.

Travemünde is in Schleswig-Holstein at the mouth of the Trave on the Bay of Lübeck (Baltic Sea), Lübeck’s north-easternmost district, about 15 kilometres from the city centre. Coordinates: 53° 57′ N, 10° 52′ E.
The district covers 41.31 km² with about 337 inhabitants per km² and lies at about 3 metres above sea level. The postcode is 23570.
The district comprises Alt-Travemünde, the Priwall peninsula and the three villages of Brodten, Teutendorf and Ivendorf, incorporated in 1935.
For its beach and seaside resort, the Old Lighthouse of 1539 (Germany’s oldest surviving lighthouse), the barque Passat, the Skandinavienkai ferry port and Travemünde Week (since 1889).

abschnitte.x: Travemünde was finally bought by Lübeck in 1329 and was incorporated as a district in 1913.

Anyone swimming in the Baltic Sea sometimes meets jellyfish in summer. Most are harmless – only one stings. Which one that is, how to identify all species, and what helps if it happens.

abschnitte.s: What are jellyfish conditions like today?
abschnitte.x: rather low Outside the warm months, or with cool water, jellyfish rarely drift close to shore. Water temperature: 16,5 °C Wind direction: 129° This is an estimate from water temperature, wind direction and season – not a measurement and not a sighting report; there is no official jellyfish count. What counts is a look into the water or the DLRG station on the beach.

abschnitte.s: Which jellyfish live in the Baltic Sea? Species ID
abschnitte.x: These are the species bathers meet most often on the German Baltic coast – the same from Travemünde via Fehmarn to Rügen: Species How to identify Noticeable sting? Moon jellyfish (Aurelia aurita) transparent, 20–30 cm, four ring-shaped markings in the centre – pink to violet in females no – its stinging cells cannot penetrate human skin Lion’s mane jellyfish (Cyanea capillata) bell dark red to yellow, up to 1 m, long fine tentacles yes – burns like stinging nettles, avoid the tentacles Stalked jellyfish (Becherqualle) small (approx. 3 cm wide, 5 cm tall), bell grey, yellow or brown has stinging capsules; hardly relevant for bathers given its size Sea walnut (comb jelly) only approx. 1 cm, transparent to milky, glows in the dark no – comb jellies have no stinging cells Species and features per ostsee.de (“Jellyfish in the Baltic Sea”).

The moon jellyfish (Aurelia aurita) is the most common jellyfish in the Baltic Sea. It is transparent and easy to recognise by the four ring-shaped markings in its centre. It is harmless to humans – its stinging cells cannot penetrate the skin. If you meet one while swimming, you can simply let it drift past.

abschnitte.s: The only one that stings: the lion’s mane jellyfish
abschnitte.x: Only one species stings noticeably: the lion’s mane jellyfish (Cyanea capillata), often called the fire jellyfish. It is yellowish-brown with long, fine tentacles. Its venom burns on the skin much like stinging nettles. It is not deadly, but it is unpleasant. People with allergies can have stronger reactions – a rash, dizziness, nausea or breathing difficulties; then they need medical help.

Most jellyfish drift in the bay in late summer, when the water is at its warmest. Onshore wind then pushes them towards the beach, where they gather along the shoreline. After calm, warm days you are more likely to come across them.

If you touch a fire jellyfish, do not rub the spot and do not rinse it with fresh water – that triggers more stinging cells. Gently scrape off any clinging tentacles with a card or with sand and rinse the skin with salt water. For a strong or allergic reaction, the local doctors and pharmacies can help.

If a lot of jellyfish are visibly drifting in the water, it is better to keep your distance or move to another spot. For how things currently look on the beach, see beach and water with the latest data. verified on 18 July 2026 Source: ostsee.de “fire jellyfish” · species and first aid

abschnitte.s: Are jellyfish in the Baltic Sea dangerous?
abschnitte.x: Most are not. The common moon jellyfish is harmless to humans. Only the fire jellyfish stings: its touch burns on the skin but is not deadly. For people with allergies it can trigger stronger reactions.

abschnitte.s: What does a fire jellyfish look like?
abschnitte.x: The fire jellyfish (lion’s mane jellyfish, Cyanea capillata) is yellowish-brown with long, fine tentacles. The venom sits on these threads and burns on the skin like stinging nettles.

abschnitte.s: What should I do after touching a jellyfish?
abschnitte.x: Do not rub the spot and do not rinse with fresh water, as that triggers more stinging cells. Gently scrape off tentacles with a card or sand and rinse with salt water. For a strong or allergic reaction, see a doctor.

abschnitte.s: When are there the most jellyfish?
abschnitte.x: Mainly in late summer, when the water is warm. Onshore wind then drives the jellyfish towards the beach, where they gather along the shore.

No. The moon jellyfish does have stinging cells, but they cannot penetrate human skin – it is harmless to humans. It is the most common and most harmless jellyfish in the Baltic Sea, easy to recognise by the four ring-shaped markings in its centre.

abschnitte.s: Which jellyfish live in the Baltic Sea?
abschnitte.x: Most common are the harmless moon jellyfish and the stinging lion’s mane jellyfish. There are also the small stalked jellyfish and the sea walnut – a comb jelly without any stinging cells that glows in the dark.

abschnitte.s: What are the pink jellyfish in the Baltic Sea?
abschnitte.x: Usually moon jellyfish: in females, the four ring-shaped reproductive organs in the centre of the bell are pink to violet. These pink-shimmering jellyfish are harmless to humans.

abschnitte.s: Are there jellyfish in the Baltic Sea right now?
abschnitte.x: There is no official jellyfish count. Rule of thumb: jellyfish are most likely in summer and late summer with warm water, especially when onshore wind pushes them towards the beach. The conditions estimate at the top of this page derives this from current weather data; what counts is a look into the water or the DLRG station on site.

abschnitte.s: Does this also apply to Fehmarn, Rügen and other Baltic beaches?
abschnitte.x: Yes. Moon jellyfish, lion’s mane and the other species occur along the entire German Baltic coast – Travemünde, Fehmarn, Rügen or Usedom. The rules of thumb on season, onshore wind and first aid apply everywhere.
Baltic or North Sea – the two German coasts compared directly. Travemünde lies on the Baltic Sea, in the Lübeck Bay. This overview shows where they differ in tides, salinity, depth and bathing.

abschnitte.s: Baltic or North Sea – the quick overview
abschnitte.x: The Baltic Sea is an almost fully landlocked inland sea. It connects to the North Sea and the Atlantic only through the Danish straits – the Little and Great Belt and the Øresund. The North Sea, by contrast, is an open marginal sea of the Atlantic, wide open to the ocean. Almost every other difference follows from this one: tides, salinity and waves.

On the North Sea, the tides shape the day: the tidal range is 2 to 3.5 metres, and twice a day the sea retreats far across the Wadden Sea. On the Baltic almost none of this is felt – the tidal range is only about 15 centimetres. Here the water level is driven more by wind than by tides.

The North Sea carries the full salinity of the Atlantic: about 35 grams of salt per litre. The Baltic is much less salty, because many rivers add fresh water and the exchange with the ocean is limited. Off Schleswig-Holstein the salinity is around 15 to 18 grams per litre and drops further east – experts call it brackish water. Baltic water therefore tastes noticeably less salty.

The North Sea is on average a good 90 metres deep, the Baltic shallower at about 55 metres. The coasts look different too: the Baltic coast in Schleswig-Holstein is shaped by firths, bodden lagoons and steep cliffs – the Brodten cliff near Travemünde is an example of an active cliff. The North Sea coast is flat and defined by sand, mudflats and marshland.

For bathers, character matters most: the Baltic is gentler, the waves usually calm, the flat beaches family-friendly. The North Sea is rougher and windier, with stronger surf and wide mudflats – ideal for water sports such as surfing or kiting. Both have their appeal, just a different one.

Travemünde lies on the western Baltic, in the Lübeck Bay – calm water, a fine sandy beach and gentle waves rather than heavy surf. For beach sections and water quality see Beach and water , and for current readings see Water temperature . verified on 10 July 2026 Source: Wikipedia “Baltic Sea” and “North Sea”, ostsee.de – figures on tides, salinity and depth

abschnitte.s: Is Travemünde on the Baltic or the North Sea?
abschnitte.x: Travemünde lies on the Baltic Sea, in the Lübeck Bay at the western edge of the sea. The North Sea only begins beyond Schleswig-Holstein on the west coast.

abschnitte.s: Which is saltier, the Baltic or the North Sea?
abschnitte.x: The North Sea is much saltier at around 35 grams of salt per litre. Off Schleswig-Holstein the Baltic reaches only about 15 to 18 grams and becomes less salty further east (brackish water).

abschnitte.s: Are there tides on the Baltic Sea?
abschnitte.x: Barely. The Baltic tidal range is about 15 centimetres and is not noticeable day to day. The North Sea, by contrast, has a tidal range of 2 to 3.5 metres with its famous Wadden Sea.

abschnitte.s: Why is the Baltic calmer than the North Sea?
abschnitte.x: The Baltic is an almost landlocked inland sea with a small tidal range and usually gentler waves. The North Sea is an open marginal sea of the Atlantic and therefore rougher and windier.
In summer the shallower Baltic often warms up faster along the coast than the deeper North Sea. Exact figures depend on the day, the wind and the location.

abschnitte.t: The salinity of the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.x: Anyone swimming in the Baltic tastes it: it is far less salty than other seas. Barely any salt crust on the skin, a mild taste in the mouth. Why that is – explained briefly and with evidence, with a look at the Bay of Lübeck off Travemünde.

abschnitte.t: The salinity of the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: How salty is the Baltic Sea?
abschnitte.x: The world’s oceans, and the North Sea too, contain around 35 grams of salt per litre of water. The Baltic is much milder: in Schleswig-Holstein the salinity is only about 15 to 17 grams per litre, and on the Polish coast just 8 to 10 grams. Roughly speaking, the western Baltic holds only about half as much salt as the North Sea – and even less further east.

abschnitte.t: The salinity of the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Why so little salt? Two reasons
abschnitte.x: A narrow door to the North Sea The Baltic is linked to the salty North Sea only through the narrow straits between Denmark and Sweden. Little salt-rich water flows in through this bottleneck. Plenty of fresh water from rivers At the same time, large rivers such as the Oder, Vistula and Neman feed in enormous amounts of fresh water, diluting the sea water ever further. Little fresh salt coming in, plenty of fresh water flowing in – that balance is what gives the Baltic its low salt concentration.

abschnitte.t: The salinity of the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Brackish water – between river and sea
abschnitte.x: This mix of salt and fresh water is called brackish water. That makes the Baltic one of the largest brackish seas in the world. And the mix is not the same everywhere: the salinity falls steadily from west to east – from the transition to the North Sea all the way into the innermost Gulfs of Bothnia and Finland, where the water is almost fresh.

abschnitte.t: The salinity of the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: What does that mean for swimming?
abschnitte.x: Less salt means less buoyancy: you do not float as easily in the Baltic as in salt-rich seas. In return, barely any salt crust is left on the skin after a swim, and the water tastes milder. The wildlife is special too – only species that cope with the low salinity live here. Some sea creatures also stay smaller in the Baltic than in the North Sea.

abschnitte.t: The salinity of the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.x: Travemünde sits on the western Baltic, in the Bay of Lübeck – here the salinity is higher than further east, but still only about half that of the North Sea. abschnitte.s: How much salt does the Baltic Sea have?
abschnitte.x: About 15 to 17 grams of salt per litre in Schleswig-Holstein, and just 8 to 10 grams on the Polish coast. For comparison: the North Sea and the ocean contain around 35 grams per litre.

abschnitte.t: The salinity of the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Why is the Baltic less salty than the North Sea?
abschnitte.x: Because it is linked to the North Sea only through the narrow straits between Denmark and Sweden, so little salt water flows in, and because large rivers such as the Oder, Vistula and Neman feed in a lot of fresh water.

abschnitte.t: The salinity of the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.x: Brackish water is a mix of salt and fresh water with a salinity between that of the sea and a river. The Baltic is one of the largest brackish seas in the world.

abschnitte.t: The salinity of the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Does Baltic salinity decrease towards the east?
abschnitte.x: Yes. The salinity falls steadily from west to east – from the transition to the North Sea into the innermost Gulfs of Bothnia and Finland, where the water is almost fresh.

abschnitte.t: The salinity of the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Can you float better in the Baltic than in the North Sea?
abschnitte.x: No, rather less well. Less salt means less buoyancy – the less salty Baltic supports the body slightly less than the saltier North Sea.

abschnitte.t: Ebb and flow in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.x: Are there tides in the Baltic Sea? The short answer: yes, but barely noticeable. Why that is – and what really moves the water level off Travemünde.

abschnitte.t: Ebb and flow in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Are there tides in the Baltic Sea?
abschnitte.x: Yes, but very weak. The difference between low and high tide – the tidal range – is about 10 to 15 centimetres in the Baltic Sea, in places around 30 centimetres. For comparison: on the North Sea it is 2 to 3.5 metres. That is why you barely notice the tides in everyday life on the Baltic.

abschnitte.t: Ebb and flow in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Why are the tides so weak?
abschnitte.x: The Baltic is an almost enclosed inland sea. It is connected to the North Sea only through the narrow Danish straits. Because ebb and flow change roughly every six hours, not enough water can flow in and out through these bottlenecks in such a short time. The tidal wave stays outside, so to speak – and the inland sea rises and falls only minimally.

abschnitte.t: Ebb and flow in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: What really moves the water level: the wind
abschnitte.x: On the Baltic it is not the moon but the wind that makes the water level. Onshore wind and wind set-up can raise the water by more than a metre – up to a storm surge. Offshore wind, by contrast, lets the level drop. Air pressure plays a part too: a low raises the water level, a high pushes it down. These weather-driven swings are many times larger on the Baltic than the actual tidal effect.

abschnitte.t: Ebb and flow in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: What does this mean for Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: No mudflat walking as on the North Sea – off Travemünde there is always enough water for swimming, sailing and surfing. No one here has to keep an eye on the tides. What matters is the weather: the current gauge and the storm-surge forecast are shown on Water level .

abschnitte.t: Ebb and flow in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.x: Without disruptive tides, swimming in the Baltic mainly comes down to one number: the water temperature. The current live value and the forecast for the coming days are shown on Water temperature . verified on 10 July 2026 Sources: t-online, ostsee4young · Wikipedia “Tides” · tidal range and causes

abschnitte.t: Ebb and flow in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Are there tides in the Baltic Sea?
abschnitte.x: Yes, but very weak. There are tides, but the difference between low and high water is only about 10 to 15 centimetres – so small that you barely notice it in everyday life.

abschnitte.t: Ebb and flow in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: How big is the tidal range in the Baltic Sea?
abschnitte.x: The tidal range – the height difference between low and high tide – is about 10 to 15 centimetres in the Baltic, in places around 30 centimetres. On the North Sea, by contrast, it is 2 to 3.5 metres.

abschnitte.t: Ebb and flow in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Why does the Baltic Sea have almost no tides?
abschnitte.x: The Baltic is an almost enclosed inland sea, connected to the North Sea only through the narrow Danish straits. Through these bottlenecks not enough water can flow in and out within the six-hour tidal cycle.

abschnitte.t: Ebb and flow in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: What changes the water level on the Baltic Sea?
abschnitte.x: Mainly the wind. Onshore wind and wind set-up can raise the water by more than a metre (storm surge), offshore wind lets it drop. Air pressure also plays a part – these swings are larger than the actual tides.

abschnitte.t: Ebb and flow in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Can you walk on mudflats on the Baltic Sea?
abschnitte.x: No. Because the tides are so weak, no mudflats fall dry as on the North Sea. Off Travemünde there is always enough water for swimming, sailing and surfing.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.x: Baltic Sea · Vibrio vulnificus · bathing with wounds

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.x: Vibrio bacteria occur naturally in the Baltic Sea – in warm, low-salt brackish water they multiply strongly in midsummer. For healthy bathers without open wounds this is harmless, and there is no general bathing ban. It becomes serious for certain risk groups: anyone with an open wound and a pre-existing condition should avoid warm seawater.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.x: Multiplication unlikely The water is cooler than 18 °C – below this threshold vibrios barely multiply. Water temperature: 16,5 °C This is an assessment based on the measured water temperature – NOT a measurement of bacteria. The state does not routinely test bathing waters for vibrios, so the number of germs cannot be derived from it.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: What does the EU model say for our bay?
abschnitte.x: The EU health agency ECDC calculates daily how favourable the environmental conditions for vibrios are – from water temperature and salinity. For the Bay of Lübeck it currently looks like this: Index off the Trave estuary 5.81 / 30 0 in the lower part of the scale 30 Model date 29/07/2026 The index rates environmental conditions only. It is not a measured germ count and says nothing about an individual’s infection risk. A higher value means the bacteria find better conditions to multiply. The value applies to the nearest model cell off the Trave estuary. Right at the beach the computation grid is land – the model returns no values there. It opens on the Baltic overview; Travemünde sits at the southern end of the Bay of Lübeck, so you need to zoom in. Loading fetches data from ecdc.europa.eu. · Open in a new tab ↗

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.x: Vibrios are rod-shaped bacteria that occur naturally in saline water – long known as a normal component of the North and Baltic Seas. In Schleswig-Holstein three species relevant to humans are mainly detected: Vibrio vulnificus, Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Vibrio cholerae (not the cholera-causing types). They prefer shallow, quickly warmed water in the Baltic, the Schlei and river estuaries – brackish water with moderate salinity.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Why the Baltic Sea in particular?
abschnitte.x: Because two conditions come together here: warmth and little salt. Vibrios prefer a salinity well below that of the North Sea or Mediterranean – the low-salt Baltic matches that exactly. Add temperature: according to the German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment, vibrios multiply markedly from about 18 °C, with a particularly high risk from 20 °C. Shallow bays such as those off Travemünde warm into exactly this range in midsummer – the current water temperature is therefore the best indicator.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: How do infections happen – and how not?
abschnitte.x: There are two routes: through wounds and through raw seafood . When bathing or wading, the bacteria can enter through even the smallest skin injuries; ear infections are also described. The second route is eating raw or insufficiently cooked seafood such as oysters, mussels, prawns or fish. Important: there is no person-to-person transmission, and swallowing seawater is not the typical route.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Who really needs to take care?
abschnitte.x: Not all bathers are equally affected. The state of Schleswig-Holstein names these groups in particular: People with open or poorly healing wounds – the decisive factor Older people with a weakened immune system People with liver disease People with diabetes mellitus People with alcohol dependency People with immunosuppressive conditions or therapies (such as cancer) For healthy bathers without wounds: normal time in the water is considered harmless. A general bathing ban for the North and Baltic Seas is not indicated according to the state, because there is no danger to the general population.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.x: With open or poorly healing wounds, stay out of warm seawater – including wading. This applies especially with the pre-existing conditions listed above. Cover fresh wounds, even small cuts or scratched insect bites, before bathing – or postpone the swim. Do not eat seafood raw and cook it thoroughly – oysters, mussels, prawns and fish. Rinse and dry wounds well after bathing. Above 20 °C, decide more consciously: the shallow, heated shore zone is the warmest part.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Symptoms: how to recognise an infection
abschnitte.x: The time between contact and first symptoms is short – usually 12 to 72 hours. With a wound infection the site hurts strikingly badly, reddens and swells; the state describes that wound infections take a very serious course in more than half of cases, with deep skin and tissue destruction up to blood poisoning. After eating raw seafood, nausea, diarrhoea and cramps dominate, in severe cases also sepsis.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: What to do if you suspect an infection
abschnitte.x: Seek medical help immediately – the course can be rapid. One sentence matters at the doctor’s: “I was swimming in the Baltic Sea.” Only then will they test specifically for vibrios. Detected early, the infections are treatable with antibiotics, even in at-risk patients. Doctors report suspected cases to the health authority under § 6 of the German Infection Protection Act. Addresses are on our page Doctors and pharmacies ; in an emergency call 112.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Does “excellent bathing water quality” say anything about vibrios?
abschnitte.x: No – and that is the most common misconception. The official EU classification of Travemünde’s two bathing waters (Kurstrand and Priwall) is based on measuring E. coli and intestinal enterococci, i.e. faecal germs. Vibrios are not included: they are natural marine bacteria and are not routinely sampled as part of bathing water monitoring. An excellent rating therefore does not mean “no vibrios” – both statements stand side by side. More on water quality under Beach and water .

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: How widespread are vibrios in Schleswig-Holstein?
abschnitte.x: The state does not sample routinely but repeatedly runs research projects. In the 2025 project, two samples were taken at each of 36 bathing sites; vibrios were detected in 64 of the 72 samples, at concentrations between 1 and 120 CFU per millilitre. Above all this shows: the bacteria are a normal part of the water, and their detection alone is not an alarm signal. Whether concentrations rise long-term due to warmer seas cannot currently be derived from the data, according to the state – though it is considered possible. abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Can you still swim in Travemünde despite vibrios?
abschnitte.x: Yes. For healthy people without open wounds, bathing in the Baltic is considered harmless; a general bathing ban is not indicated according to the state of Schleswig-Holstein, because there is no danger to the general population. Caution applies to risk groups with wounds.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: From what water temperature are vibrios active?
abschnitte.x: They multiply markedly from about 18 °C, and from 20 °C there is a particularly high risk according to the Federal Institute for Risk Assessment. The state of Schleswig-Holstein names the mark of around 20 °C at which Vibrio vulnificus is activated. They remain active for a while even when the temperature drops below that again.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: How do you get infected with vibrios?
abschnitte.x: Through wounds while bathing or wading – even the smallest skin injuries suffice – and by eating raw or insufficiently cooked seafood such as oysters, mussels, prawns or fish. Ear infections are also described. Vibrios are not transmitted from person to person.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Who belongs to the risk group?
abschnitte.x: Above all people with open or poorly healing wounds, older people with a weakened immune system, and people with liver disease, diabetes mellitus, alcohol dependency or immunosuppressive conditions and therapies.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: What are the symptoms of a vibrio infection?
abschnitte.x: Symptoms usually appear 12 to 72 hours after contact. With wound infections the site hurts strikingly badly, reddens and swells; severe courses with deep tissue damage up to blood poisoning are possible. After eating raw seafood, nausea, diarrhoea and cramps dominate.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: What to do if a wound hurts after bathing?
abschnitte.x: Seek medical help immediately and explicitly mention that you were swimming in the Baltic Sea – only then will they test specifically for vibrios. Detected early, the infections are treatable with antibiotics. In an emergency call 112.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Is the bathing water in Travemünde tested for vibrios?
abschnitte.x: No, there is no routine sampling for vibrios. Official bathing water monitoring measures E. coli and intestinal enterococci. However, the state repeatedly runs research projects; in 2025 vibrios were detected in 64 of 72 samples at 36 bathing sites.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Does “excellent water quality” mean there are no vibrios?
abschnitte.x: No. The EU classification is based on faecal germs (E. coli, enterococci) and says nothing about vibrios, which are natural marine bacteria. Both statements can be true at the same time.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Are vibrios new to the Baltic Sea?
abschnitte.x: No. They have long been known as a natural component of the North and Baltic Seas. What is new is that warm summers more often favour the conditions for them to multiply; so far the state does not derive a robust trend of rising concentrations from its data.

abschnitte.t: Vibrio bacteria in the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.s: Are children or dogs particularly at risk?
abschnitte.x: For healthy children the same rules apply as for adults: without open wounds bathing is harmless, fresh grazes are better covered or the swim postponed. The state makes no statement on pets – with open wounds on an animal, restraint is sensible; if in doubt ask a vet.

abschnitte.t: The history of the beach chair
abschnitte.x: Invented 1882 · Wilhelm Bartelmann · Baltic Sea

abschnitte.t: The history of the beach chair
abschnitte.x: No Baltic beach without it – the beach chair. It was invented in 1882 by a basket maker from Rostock who was asked to build a sheltered seat for an ailing woman. How it came about, why there are so many of them today, and what sets Baltic and North Sea chairs apart.

abschnitte.t: The history of the beach chair
abschnitte.x: The Rostock master basket maker Wilhelm Bartelmann (1845–1930) is regarded as the inventor of the beach chair. As imperial court basket maker he ran his own workshop in Rostock – and in 1882 created a piece of furniture that remains part of the scenery on every Baltic beach to this day.

abschnitte.t: The history of the beach chair
abschnitte.x: In the spring of 1882 Elfriede von Maltzahn, who suffered from rheumatism, asked Bartelmann for a sheltered seat on the beach that would let her linger in the fresh air. Bartelmann wove the first “beach chair” from willow and cane – a single-seater with a tall, curved hood that kept off wind and sun.

abschnitte.t: The history of the beach chair
abschnitte.x: The single-seater caught on quickly, and a two-seater with footrests, an awning and fold-out side tables soon followed. Bartelmann and his wife opened the first beach-chair rental near the lighthouse in Warnemünde – the start of a success story all along the coast.

abschnitte.t: The history of the beach chair
abschnitte.x: Bartelmann never filed a patent on his invention. Other basket makers copied the beach chair, and so it spread rapidly across the entire Baltic and North Sea coasts. The regions still differ in build to this day: Baltic chairs usually have a square roof, North Sea chairs a rounded one.

abschnitte.t: The history of the beach chair
abschnitte.x: At Travemünde’s spa beach the beach chairs are part of the scenery – in long rows between promenade and water. To rent one, you’ll find providers, prices and locations in the beach chair guide ; more about the beach itself is under Beach and water . verified on 10 July 2026 Source: Wikipedia “Strandkorb” · invention and history

abschnitte.t: The best time to visit Travemünde
abschnitte.x: When is Travemünde worth it? That depends on what you seek: swimming weather, quiet or programme. This page answers with data – official overnight-stay figures, measured water and air temperatures and the real events calendar, month by month.

abschnitte.t: The best time to visit Travemünde
abschnitte.x: For swimming July and August: water around 20–20 °C, the most summer days. For quiet January to February: only about 33 % of the summer crowds. For programme October: the most events in the calendar (210). The best time to visit Travemünde is a question of priorities. For swimming, July and August are the safest bet: the Baltic then averages 20.3 to 20.3 °C (measured since 2023), and the local DWD record shows the highest daily means for both months. But that is also when it is busiest: July averages 281,133 overnight stays in the official Lübeck statistics (mean 2022–2024). If you want the bay to yourself, come in January: only 92,285 overnight stays – about 33 % of the summer figure – with an empty beach and storm-surge drama. The honest compromise is May/June and September: May and June bring the most light of the year at about 8.0 sunshine hours a day, while September keeps the water mostly above 16 °C as crowds fall away. Travemünde Week in late July is the special case – sporting highlight and busiest stretch at once. Sources: Lübeck statistics office, DWD local record, Open-Meteo water measurements.

On the Trave and Baltic · verified · from Travemünde only

Take the helm yourself or go with a skipper: in Travemünde you can hire a motorboat – small ones up to 15 hp even without a licence –, take a harbour tour on the MS Hanse or charter a party boat for a celebration, and rent stand-up paddle boards at the beach. This page deliberately lists only operators that start in or from Travemünde – each individually verified, with address, source and verification date.
Passenger ship · harbour tour · party charter

The town’s passenger ship: “The charming hour” as a one-hour harbour tour, plus the panorama cruise to Lübeck (several times daily). For celebrations, weddings and company parties the MS Hanse can be chartered exclusively – up to 300 guests in the salon and on deck. Address: Überseebrücke 2, Travepromenade, 23570 Travemünde hanse-travemuende.de ↗ Open in map ↗ Motorboat hire – no licence needed

By its own account the only rental in town without a boating licence: two 15-hp motorboats (“Sunrise” and “Sundown”) for up to five people, bookable from two hours. The base is right next to the Priwall ferry. Address: Travepromenade, neben der Priwall-Personenfähre, 23570 Travemünde bootszentrum.jimdoweb.com ↗ ☎ 0173 6600544 Open in map ↗ Motorboat hire (licence required)

Larger self-drive motorboats (including Finnmaster, Flipper and Bella) for trips on the Trave and in Lübeck Bay. The base at the Prinzenbrücke cites over 40 years of watersports experience. Address: Vorderreihe 59a / Prinzenbrücke, 23570 Travemünde hurricane-bootsvermietung.de ↗ Open in map ↗ Stand-up paddling – self-service hire

Automated SUP station at the Aktionsstrand: book a board online for your preferred time, open the locker via a link on your phone and paddle off without waiting. Open daily in season. Address: Aktionsstrand, neben der Lighthouse Lounge, 23570 Travemünde kolula.com ↗ Open in map ↗ verified on 1 July 2026

Licence-free up to 15 hp: on the Trave and Baltic, motorboats up to 15 hp (11.03 kW) may be operated without a boating licence. Bootsvermietung Travemünde on the Travepromenade specialises in this; larger boats (Hurricane) require a licence. Party boat: for celebrations the MS Hanse can be chartered exclusively – up to 300 guests, salon plus deck. In Travemünde this is the classic “party boat” for weddings, birthdays and company parties. Panorama cruise both ways: the scheduled Travemünde–Lübeck run (about 1.5 hours, several times daily in summer) goes there and back – you can also board in Lübeck and arrive in Travemünde. SUP without booking in person: the kolula station at the Aktionsstrand is fully automated – book a board online, open the locker via phone, paddle off. No course, no staff to wait for. Deliberately left out: the classic harbour and canal tours by Quandt-Linie and Böttcher Schifffahrt depart from Lübeck, not Travemünde; the nearest pedal boats are in Timmendorfer Strand. This page only lists what starts in or from Travemünde.

abschnitte.x: Yes. Bootsvermietung Travemünde on the Travepromenade (next to the Priwall ferry) rents out 15-hp motorboats that may be operated on the Trave and Baltic without a boating licence – for up to five people, bookable from two hours.

Coastal cliff · over 4 km · up to 20 m high

North of Travemünde the coast breaks off: the Brodten cliff is a coastal cliff over four kilometres long, up to 20 metres high, between Travemünde and Niendorf. Along the top a walking and cycling path follows the edge, below lies the beach – and the whole coast retreats a little year by year. A trip for hikers, bird lovers and anyone who wants to see the Baltic from above.
> 4 km Length of the cliff up to 20 m Height above the beach 50–100 cm Retreat per year ≈ 2,600 Sand-martin nest tubes verified on 1 July 2026

The path runs along the top edge between Travemünde and Niendorf/Ostsee – a good four kilometres with a wide view over Lübeck Bay. You can start in Travemünde (at the northern end of the Kurstrand) and walk to Niendorf or vice versa; the bus is handy for the way back. Below by the water a beach section runs along, but it is not continuously passable at high water and after landslides – the top is safer and offers more to see. The natural beach below the cliff is free of charge, by the way – a beach fee is only charged on the managed sections Stadtstrand, Priwall beach and Grünstrand.
From the north end of the Kurstrand the path climbs to the cliff edge – after a few minutes the view opens across the bay. Open in map ↗
A stop halfway, right at the edge – with a garden and a view over the Baltic. Open in map ↗
The highest stretch of the cliff: up to 20 metres above the Baltic, with sand martins nesting in the face in spring. Open in map ↗

Fishing cutters, smokehouse and pier – from here the bus takes you back to Travemünde. Open in map ↗ Map geometry: OpenStreetMap (ODbL) · stations and opening hours: German Tourism Knowledge Graph (GNTB/DZT), data by TA.SH · as of 2026-07-07 To the Kurstrand and the beach sections →

The cliff is a living coast: wind, waves and rain erode it by an average of 50 to 100 centimetres per year. Between 1810 and 1900 the coast lost around 100 metres. This natural dynamic cannot be permanently stopped – the break-off edges are real, so both above and below: keep your distance from the edge and take barriers seriously. It is exactly this erosion that keeps exposing glacial boulders and fossils on the beach. After autumn storms it is worth checking the drift line below the cliff edge – with a little luck you can find amber there.

One of Europe’s largest sand-martin colonies breeds in the open cliff faces – around 2,600 nest tubes in the sand. The cliff is designated a European bird protection area. From the paths the activity can be watched well without disturbing the breeding walls – please stay on the paths.

The cliff lies on the western edge of Lübeck Bay and faces east over the open water – in the morning the sun stands over the sea and bathes the walls in warm light. When exactly the sun rises and sets today and where to stand best is shown by the sun module on the home page. To the sun module on the home page →

abschnitte.x: At 50 to 100 centimetres of retreat per year, a calculated 74 to 148 metres of cliff have gone since the Prussian survey of 1878 – the shoreline mapped then now lies far out in the bay. abschnitte.s: How long is the Brodten cliff?
abschnitte.x: The coastal cliff is over four kilometres long and up to 20 metres high. It runs between Lübeck-Travemünde and Niendorf/Ostsee along Lübeck Bay.

abschnitte.s: Can you hike along the Brodten cliff?
abschnitte.x: Yes. Along the top a walking and cycling path runs the good four kilometres between Travemünde and Niendorf, with a wide view over the Baltic. The bus is handy for the way back.

abschnitte.s: How strong is the coastal erosion at the cliff?
abschnitte.x: On average the coast retreats by about 50 to 100 centimetres per year; between 1810 and 1900 it was around 100 metres. The natural erosion cannot be permanently stopped – keep your distance from the break-off edge.

abschnitte.s: What animals live at the Brodten cliff?
abschnitte.x: One of Europe’s largest sand-martin colonies breeds in the cliff walls, with around 2,600 nest tubes. The cliff is a European bird protection area.

abschnitte.s: How do I get from Travemünde to the cliff?
abschnitte.x: From the northern end of the Kurstrand the path leads straight to the cliff; on foot or by bike you are there in a few minutes. Hikers walk the route as far as Niendorf.
Priwall · fishing harbour · close to the beach

Camping in Travemünde happens mainly on the Priwall: a long-established beach campsite is there, plus a motorhome pitch close to the beach. Those who want to stay in town itself find a motorhome site at the fishing harbour; family-friendly with a natural bathing pond is the site in Ivendorf on the edge of town. This page lists the verified sites with source and verification date – prices and vacancies are with the operator.

Location: Priwall, by the beach A long-established campsite (run by the Katt family since 1958) with around 200 pitches for caravans and tents on about 27,000 m², right by the beach on the peninsula. priwall.de ↗

Location: Mecklenburger Landstraße 49–67, Priwall Around 30 motorhome pitches close to the beach, with shops within walking distance. Season roughly from mid-April to early October. ostsee-schleswig-holstein.de ↗

Location: At the fishing harbour A site right at the fishing harbour within sight of the Skandinavienkai – only around 150 metres to the town centre and about 800 metres to the beach. Ideal for staying in the thick of it. wohnmobil-atlas.de ↗

Location: Ivendorf, edge of town A family-friendly site near Travemünde with around 200 pitches, a natural bathing pond and holiday homes and log cabins – a little quieter in the green. camping-travemuende.de ↗ verified on 1 July 2026

The Priwall sites are reached from the town centre by the Priwall ferry, which also carries bicycles. The motorhome site at the fishing harbour, by contrast, is right on the town side. Many pitches are seasonal (roughly mid-April to early October). Prices, opening and vacancies change – please check and book with the operator in advance. Wild camping and free overnight parking in a motorhome outside designated sites is not permitted on the coast.

abschnitte.s: Is there Wi-Fi at the campsite and motorhome site?
abschnitte.x: The official free “GastWLAN” guest Wi-Fi (usable without a ticket) covers the promenade, the Passathafen and the Priwall beach on the Priwall – that is, the immediate surroundings of the beach campsite and the motorhome pitch. On the sites themselves, the respective operator’s own offering applies.

abschnitte.s: Is there a campsite in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Yes. On the Priwall is the long-established Strandcamping Priwall (since 1958, the Katt family, around 200 pitches). On the edge of town there is also the family-friendly Ivendorf campsite with a natural bathing pond.

abschnitte.s: Where can you stay with a motorhome in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: On the Priwall there is a motorhome pitch (Mecklenburger Landstraße 49–67, around 30 pitches) close to the beach, and right at the fishing harbour on the town side a motorhome site, only a few minutes from the centre.

abschnitte.s: Are the campsites open all year?
abschnitte.x: Many sites are seasonal, often roughly from mid-April to early October. Exact times and vacancies change – best to check with each operator in advance.

abschnitte.s: Can you stay overnight freely in a motorhome in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: No. Wild camping and free overnight parking outside designated pitches and campsites is not permitted on the coast. Use the listed sites on the Priwall or at the fishing harbour.

abschnitte.t: The climate of Travemünde – measured in town
abschnitte.x: How warm, how sunny, how stormy is Travemünde really? This page answers with official records from the DWD station right in town (since 1940): the warmest month is July at 17.0 °C daily mean; January has the most days with gusts of 8 Beaufort or more.

abschnitte.t: The climate of Travemünde – measured in town
abschnitte.s: The climate in numbers – the short version
abschnitte.x: Travemünde sits on the Bay of Lübeck and has a typical Baltic-coast climate: mild, breezy, without extremes. In the local DWD record (temperature 1940–2001), July is the warmest month at 17.0 °C daily mean, January the coldest at 0.3 °C. The heat record is 34.8 °C (August 1992), the cold record -27.7 °C (February 1940). May and June bring the most sunshine (about 8.0 hours a day); rain days are spread remarkably evenly. Winter is stormiest: January averages 6.6 days with gusts of 8 Beaufort or more – measured up to today, as the station's wind record continues. For context: the temperature series ends in 2001; today's values run noticeably higher due to climate warming.

abschnitte.t: The climate of Travemünde – measured in town
abschnitte.s: Where the numbers come from – and where the series ends
abschnitte.x: DWD station Travemünde (ID 05078) has measured right in town since 1940. Since October 2001 it records wind only – temperature, sunshine and precipitation therefore come from the historical series 1940–2001, while gusts continue to today (daily peak gusts since 1971) and are updated here monthly. The count is days with gusts of 8 Beaufort or more. True storm days by the DWD definition – a 10-minute mean of 8 Beaufort or more – are rare in town: 20 in the 18 years 2008–2025. Present-day temperatures run about one degree above the old series due to climate warming. Current water temperatures are live on the water-temperature page. To water temperature → verified on 25 September 2026

abschnitte.t: The climate of Travemünde – measured in town
abschnitte.s: “October is when the autumn storms start – the storm month.”
abschnitte.x: Not quite. October averages 3.8 days with gusts of 8 Beaufort or more – January leads with 6.6, followed by December (5.5) and March (5.1). Midwinter is the true storm season on the Bay of Lübeck (wind record 1971–today).

abschnitte.t: The climate of Travemünde – measured in town
abschnitte.s: “It rains all the time on the Baltic.”
abschnitte.x: No – remarkably even. Between 8.6 rain days in May and 11.2 in December there is less spread than many think. Spring is the driest season – and even the wettest month is rain-free two days out of three (series 1940–2001).

abschnitte.t: The climate of Travemünde – measured in town
abschnitte.s: “It never gets really hot on the Baltic.”
abschnitte.x: Almost true. Even the series’ heat record – 34.8 °C in August 1992 – stayed below inland peaks; genuine summer days above 25 °C occurred only about 3.7 times a month in July and August. The Baltic tempers the heat – which is exactly why it is so bearable here.

abschnitte.t: The climate of Travemünde – measured in town
abschnitte.s: How warm is Travemünde in summer?
abschnitte.x: In the local DWD record (1940–2001) July is the warmest month at 17.0 °C daily mean; midsummer daytime highs are mostly around 20–22 °C. Due to climate warming, present-day summers run about one degree above these means.

abschnitte.t: The climate of Travemünde – measured in town
abschnitte.x: In May and June – with about 8.0 sunshine hours per day on average. The sunniest single month of the record was July 1994 with 372 hours.

abschnitte.t: The climate of Travemünde – measured in town
abschnitte.s: How often is it actually stormy?
abschnitte.x: Gale-force gusts are most frequent in midwinter: January averages 6.6 days with gusts of 8 Beaufort or more, June only 1.8 (wind record 1971–today). True storm days by the DWD definition, when even the 10-minute mean reaches 8 Beaufort, are rare: 20 in the 18 years 2008–2025, about 1.1 a year.

abschnitte.t: The climate of Travemünde – measured in town
abschnitte.s: What was the hottest day ever measured in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: 34.8 °C in August 1992. The cold record: -27.7 °C in February 1940, in the legendary hard winter of 1939/40.

abschnitte.x: The DWD station Travemünde has recorded wind only since October 2001. Temperature, sunshine and precipitation therefore come from the historical 1940–2001 series; peak gusts continue to be updated. Current water temperatures are live on the water-temperature page.

On the Baltic Coast Cycle Route · EuroVelo 10

Travemünde lies on one of Germany’s finest cycle routes: the Baltic Coast Cycle Route (EuroVelo 10) reaches the Trave estuary here after running along the Schleswig-Holstein coast and continues east over the Priwall. Add to that short, rewarding tours in town – along the cliff, over the Priwall or along the Trave to Lübeck. This page places the route in context and names the best tours, honestly and with a verification date.

abschnitte.s: Travemünde on the Baltic Coast Cycle Route
abschnitte.x: The Baltic Coast Cycle Route is the German section of the European long-distance route EuroVelo 10 (the “Hanseatic Route”), which runs around the Baltic for some 8,000 kilometres. From the Danish border near Flensburg it runs via Eckernförde, Kiel and the island of Fehmarn to Lübeck-Travemünde. Here the Schleswig-Holstein part ends: over the Priwall the route crosses into Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and continues to the seaside resort of Ahlbeck. Travemünde is thus a natural stage and overnight point on the route. Steilufer-Tour (Travemünde–Niendorf) Priwall-Rundweg Ostseeküsten-Radweg (D2) verified on 1 July 2026
Along the top edge of the Brodten cliff, a good four kilometres with a wide view over Lübeck Bay to Niendorf. The classic short loop. Brodten cliff →

abschnitte.s: Over the Priwall to the border
abschnitte.x: Cross on the bicycle ferry and cycle across the Priwall to the former inner-German border at the eastern tip – beach, Passat and nature reserve included. The Priwall →
Follow the water all the way into Lübeck’s old town (UNESCO World Heritage) – flat and scenic. The train makes the return easy. Day trips →

The Priwall ferry has a year-round passenger and bicycle ferry – bikes come straight across the Trave. This puts the Priwall, the Passat harbour and the route towards Mecklenburg-Vorpommern within a few minutes. The car ferry also carries bikes.

abschnitte.s: Does the Baltic Coast Cycle Route pass through Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Yes. Travemünde lies on the Baltic Coast Cycle Route, the German part of EuroVelo 10. Coming from Flensburg via Fehmarn, the route reaches the Trave estuary here and crosses over the Priwall into Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

abschnitte.s: Which bike tours are worthwhile from Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Short and rewarding are the ride along the top of the Brodten cliff to Niendorf, the loop across the Priwall to the former border, and the flat path along the Trave to Lübeck (return by train).

abschnitte.s: Can you take a bike on the Priwall ferry?
abschnitte.x: Yes. The Priwall ferry runs a year-round passenger and bicycle ferry; bikes are carried. The car ferry also takes bicycles.

Travemünde is an ideal base: Lübeck’s old town with its UNESCO World Heritage is a short train ride away, the neighbouring resorts of the Bay of Lübeck are reached by the coastal bus, the Priwall by ferry and the Brodten cliffs on foot. Here are the most rewarding trips – sorted by how you get there.

abschnitte.s: Lübeck – the old town (UNESCO World Heritage)
abschnitte.x: Getting there: Train from Travemünde Strand The Holsten Gate, seven towers, Niederegger marzipan and the Buddenbrook House: Lübeck’s old town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987 and is quickly reached by train.
Getting there: Bus (coastal line 40) The elegant neighbouring resorts of the Bay of Lübeck – promenades, a pier, the Niendorf harbour. The bus line 40 connects the resorts along the coast.

Getting there: Priwall ferry, then on foot The peninsula opposite the Vorderreihe: the museum ship Passat, a quiet natural beach, a marina and a nature reserve. A few minutes across on the Priwall ferry. All about the Priwall →

Getting there: Walk from the Kurstrand The active cliff coast north of the Kurstrand – up to 20 metres high, about four kilometres to Niendorf. A coastal classic with the Hermannshöhe viewpoint. To the Brodten cliff →

Getting there: From the Vorderreihe From April to early October excursion boats run up the Trave to the Lübeck bascule bridge – about 90 minutes of harbour and coast from the water. Operators and party boats →

abschnitte.s: Baltic Coast Cycle Route and Hanseatenweg
abschnitte.x: Getting there: By bike Travemünde lies on the Baltic Coast Cycle Route (EuroVelo 10) and the Hanseatenweg – ideal starting points for tours along the bay or towards Lübeck and Wismar. Cycling in Travemünde →

From Travemünde the coast runs north-west along the Brodten cliffs – past the Niendorf fishing harbour to the resort of Timmendorf. The three towns sit on one continuous coastal arc; on foot over the cliffs, by the coastal bus or by bike the whole chain is easy to explore.
The starting point at the mouth of the Trave – beach, Vorderreihe and the ferry to the Priwall.
The active cliff coast between the towns – a walking and cycling path on top, up to 20 metres above the Baltic.
A fishing harbour with a smokehouse and pier, quieter than its bigger neighbour – reached on foot over the cliffs or by the coastal bus.

The elegant seaside resort of the Bay of Lübeck: a wide promenade, a pier and boutiques – the end of this coastline. Live departures for train and bus are on the getting-here page . Build a whole day in the coast planner . verified on 1 July 2026

abschnitte.s: What can you do from Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Rewarding trips include Lübeck’s old town (UNESCO World Heritage) by train, the neighbouring resorts Timmendorf and Niendorf by coastal bus, the Priwall by ferry, the Brodten cliffs on foot and a harbour cruise on the Trave.

abschnitte.s: Is Lübeck’s old town a World Heritage Site?
abschnitte.x: Yes. Lübeck’s old town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987 – known for the Holsten Gate, the seven church towers and its marzipan.

abschnitte.s: Can you take a boat trip from Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Yes. From April to early October excursion boats run from the Vorderreihe up the Trave – the harbour cruise takes about 90 minutes.

Writers · painters · champions · history

Travemünde has drawn and produced writers, painters and athletes: Thomas Mann called the resort his “childhood paradise” and immortalised it in “Buddenbrooks”, Edvard Munch set up his easel here, and Travemünde is the birthplace of Peter Deilmann, whose ship became famous as the German “Traumschiff”. This page gathers the best-known names – each with a documented link to the town.

The Nobel laureate spent his boyhood summers in Travemünde as a Lübeck schoolboy and called it his “childhood paradise”. The resort appears in “Buddenbrooks” and “Tonio Kröger” – the town’s most famous literary link.
The Prague writer sat barefoot on the beach of Travemünde in the summer of 1914 – a brief but well-documented visit on one of his Baltic trips.
In the 19th century Travemünde’s casino also drew Russian authors – partly for the gambling. The casino shaped the resort’s elegant reputation for over a century and a half, until it closed in 2012.
The Norwegian painter of “The Scream” stayed on Lübeck Bay in the early 20th century and painted the Travemünde church in 1903 – one of several coastal motifs from that period.
German impressionists too captured Travemünde’s beach and resort life – part of a whole line of coastal painters the town attracted.
The future chancellor and Nobel Peace laureate fled via Travemünde by ship to Denmark in April 1933 as a young Social Democrat – his path into exile began here.
The last German emperor visited the resort in 1894 – evidence of the standing Travemünde held as a fashionable Baltic resort in the imperial era.
Born in Travemünde, he turned small freight and fishing vessels into one of Germany’s best-known cruise lines. His ship “Berlin” became famous on TV as the “Traumschiff”.
The Travemünde-born footballer won the league and the European Cup with Hamburger SV and played for the German national team.
The multiple swimming world champion and Olympic medallist grew up partly in Lübeck-Travemünde.
The Travemünde dialect poet and sexton shaped local cultural life; a fountain in town commemorates him. verified on 3 July 2026

abschnitte.x: Those born in Travemünde include the cruise-line owner Peter Deilmann (whose ship became famous as the “Traumschiff”) and the football international Peter “Eiche” Nogly. The swimming world champion Antje Buschschulte grew up there.

abschnitte.x: As a Lübeck schoolboy Thomas Mann spent his summers in Travemünde and called it his “childhood paradise”. The resort appears in his works “Buddenbrooks” and “Tonio Kröger” – the town’s most famous literary link.

abschnitte.s: Why did Russian writers come to Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: In the 19th century Travemünde had a casino that also drew Russian authors such as Dostoevsky – partly for the gambling. The casino lasted until 2012 and shaped the resort’s elegant reputation.

Among others Edvard Munch, painter of “The Scream”: he stayed on Lübeck Bay and painted the Travemünde church in 1903. German impressionists such as Gotthardt Kuehl and Ulrich Hübner also captured the resort.

abschnitte.t: Finding amber on the Baltic coast
abschnitte.x: Baltic gold · wrack line · October–March

abschnitte.t: Finding amber on the Baltic coast
abschnitte.x: Amber is fossilised tree resin – the “gold of the Baltic”. Along the Bay of Lübeck around Travemünde and at the Brodten cliff it can be found with a little knowledge: at the right time, in the right place and with an eye for the right material. What amber is, when and where the chances are best, how to tell real amber – and why, in case of doubt, a find does not belong in a pocket.

abschnitte.t: Finding amber on the Baltic coast
abschnitte.x: The high season for amber runs from October to March. The best chances come after autumn and winter storms with onshore winds, when the sea washes plenty of material onto the beach. Early risers who reach the beach before the other collectors get the fresh strandings to themselves.

abschnitte.t: Finding amber on the Baltic coast
abschnitte.x: Look where seaweed, bladderwrack, algae and driftwood have washed ashore. Among shells and flotsam, in the so-called wrack line, lies the golden-yellow stone. The Bay of Lübeck – like the Hohwacht Bay – and the cliffs supply the material: at the Brodten cliff the coast erodes and keeps releasing finds.

abschnitte.t: Finding amber on the Baltic coast
abschnitte.s: How do I recognise real amber?
abschnitte.x: Real amber is strikingly light and feels warm, not cool like stone. It floats in strongly salted water (the salt-water test) and sinks in fresh water. Rubbed, it builds an electrostatic charge and attracts small scraps of paper. Under UV light real amber fluoresces – another reliable sign.

abschnitte.t: Finding amber on the Baltic coast
abschnitte.x: Caution is essential: white phosphorus from old wartime munitions can look confusingly similar to amber. Once dry it ignites in the air by itself and burns with great heat. Such a find must never go into a pocket or into clothing. In case of doubt, place the piece in a fireproof metal tin with damp sand, kept away from clothing – and in an emergency call the rescue services.

abschnitte.t: Finding amber on the Baltic coast
abschnitte.x: Around Travemünde the beach sections below the cliffs are worth searching after a storm. Anyone wanting to combine the search with a walk will find at the Brodten cliff the eroding edge with the most material; current wind and water data are shown under Beach and water . Amber is never a guaranteed find – but with patience, timing and the right stretch of beach the chances rise noticeably. verified on 10 July 2026 Source: ostsee.de “amber” and Wikipedia · finding season, features and phosphorus warning

abschnitte.s: When is the best time for amber?
abschnitte.x: The high season runs from October to March. Chances are best after autumn and winter storms with onshore winds, early in the morning before the other collectors, once the sea has washed fresh material ashore.

abschnitte.t: Finding amber on the Baltic coast
abschnitte.s: How do I recognise real amber?
abschnitte.x: Real amber is very light, feels warm, floats in strongly salted water and sinks in fresh water. Rubbed it builds an electrostatic charge, and under UV light it fluoresces.

abschnitte.t: Finding amber on the Baltic coast
abschnitte.s: Can amber be confused with phosphorus?
abschnitte.x: Yes. White phosphorus from old wartime munitions resembles amber, can ignite in the air by itself and cause severe burns. A suspicious find does not belong in clothing but in a fireproof metal tin with damp sand.

abschnitte.t: Finding amber on the Baltic coast
abschnitte.s: Where along the Bay of Lübeck do you find amber?
abschnitte.x: Wherever seaweed, algae and driftwood lie in the wrack line. The Bay of Lübeck and the Hohwacht Bay, as well as cliffs like the Brodten cliff, supply the material the sea releases.

abschnitte.t: Finding amber on the Baltic coast
abschnitte.x: In strongly salted water amber floats or hovers just below the surface, while in fresh water it sinks. This salt-water test is a simple way to tell real amber from heavier stone.

Since 2011 Schleswig-Holstein has celebrated World Fish Roll Day on the first Saturday in May – an initiative of Ostsee-Holstein-Tourismus that celebrates fishing, maritime culture and the stand next door. The coast holds special events; in 2026 the day falls on 2 May. A good reason to work your way through Travemünde’s stands.

abschnitte.s: A short history of the fish roll
abschnitte.x: The fish roll comes from the north-German port cities of the 19th century: a quick, cheap meal for fishermen, sailors and dockworkers, eaten standing up. Because fresh fish spoils quickly, it was preserved – salted, pickled, smoked. That gave rise to matjes, Bismarck herring and rollmops, still the basis of the topped roll today. A workers’ snack became a cultural staple of the whole coast.

The honest answer: a matter of taste. We crown no “top 5” and invent no stars – if you want to choose by real ratings, the aggregate scores of the individual stands are in the places directory. Our tip: head to the fishing harbour in the morning when the cutters are back, and simply try two stands. Real Google ratings in the places directory →

“Four-masted barque”, “windjammer”, “barque” – and at the heart of it the Passat, the landmark of Travemünde. What the terms mean and what makes this ship special.

A barque is a sailing ship with at least three masts. On the forward masts it carries square sails – the rectangular sails set across the ship. On the aftermost mast, by contrast, it carries only fore-and-aft sails, set lengthways along the ship. This combination is what defines a barque and sets it apart from a full-rigged ship.

A four-masted barque is simply a barque with four masts. Larger barques are named after the number of their masts: the four-masted barque has four, the five-masted barque five. The more masts, the more sail area – and the more power from the wind for these large cargo sailers.

“Windjammer” is the collective term for the large cargo sailing ships of the 19th and early 20th centuries. Under sail these ships carried bulk goods across the oceans, at a time when steamships were slowly replacing them. The Passat, too, is one of these windjammers.

The Passat was built in 1911 by Blohm und Voss in Hamburg for the shipping company F. Laeisz – together with her sister ship, the Peking. She is one of the “Eight Sisters”, the last eight four-masted barques of the Laeisz fleet, whose ship names all began with “P”. Her steel hull is around 115 metres long and 14.3 metres wide. On the saltpetre run she sailed around Cape Horn to Chile.

In 1959 Lübeck saved the Passat from being scrapped. Since her last major refit in 1998 she has been moored as a museum ship at the Priwall in Travemünde, open to visitors. More on the ships of the Trave estuary under Ships and on the landmark on the shore under the Maritim . verified on 10 July 2026 Source: Wikipedia “Passat (Schiff, 1911)” · construction and history

A four-masted barque is a sailing ship with four masts in the rig of a barque: square sails on the forward masts (across the ship) and only fore-and-aft sails on the aftermost mast (lengthways). One example is the Passat in Travemünde.

abschnitte.s: What is the difference between a barque and a full-rigged ship?
abschnitte.x: On a full-rigged ship all masts carry square sails. On a barque, by contrast, the aftermost mast carries only fore-and-aft sails while the forward masts carry square sails. It is this last mast that tells the two rigs apart.
“Windjammer” is the collective term for the large cargo sailing ships of the 19th and early 20th centuries, which carried bulk goods across the oceans under sail. The Passat is one such windjammer.
The Passat is moored as a museum ship at the Priwall in Travemünde, at the mouth of the Trave where it meets the Baltic Sea. She is open to visitors there.
The Passat was built in 1911 by Blohm und Voss in Hamburg for the shipping company F. Laeisz. She is one of the last eight four-masted barques of the Laeisz fleet, the “Eight Sisters”.

Travemünde holds more records and curiosities than the beach lets on: Germany’s oldest surviving lighthouse (1539), a beacon on a high-rise, and a past as a French town (1811–1813). Here are the most surprising fun facts – each with a source, no invented numbers.

Germany’s oldest surviving lighthouse – It stands in Travemünde: built in 1539 by Dutch masons, 31 metres tall – a cultural monument since 1922. The tower’s full story . But it no longer shines – The Old Lighthouse has been out of service since 1972. The reason: the neighbouring Maritim high-rise blocked the tower. The beacon now sits on a high-rise – Since 1974 it has shone from the 119-metre Maritim building – with a focal height of 114.7 metres, the tallest building in Schleswig-Holstein. Travemünde was once France – From 1811 to 1813 the town belonged to the French Empire under Napoleon. Its own town until 1913 – Only then was Travemünde incorporated into Lübeck as a district – before that it was an independent town at the mouth of the Trave. The German Baltic’s second seaside resort – As early as 1802 Travemünde was recognised as a seaside resort – after Heiligendamm (1793) the second on the entire German Baltic coast. Travemünde Week began with a bottle of Rotspon – In 1889 the Hamburg merchants Wentzel and Dröge raced off Travemünde – the winner got a bottle of Lübeck Rotspon. It grew into one of the largest sailing events in the world. A tall ship from 1911 as the landmark – The barque Passat was launched in 1911 and lies today as a museum ship on the Priwall – its masts rise about 56 metres.

63 years of a casino – From 1949 to 2012 a casino operated in Travemünde; today the building houses a hotel. Almost at sea level – Travemünde sits on average just about 3 metres above sea level – though tides barely matter on the nearly tide-free Baltic. Sources: Wikipedia (Lübeck-Travemünde), Wikidata, official Travemünde Week site. verified on 1 July 2026

Travemünde combines beach and seaside-resort tradition (since 1802) with maritime records: Germany’s oldest surviving lighthouse (1539), the museum ship Passat (1911) and the Skandinavienkai ferry port. Since 1913 it has been a district of Lübeck.

abschnitte.s: Why does the Old Lighthouse no longer shine?
abschnitte.x: Because the Maritim high-rise, completed in 1974, blocked the tower. The Old Lighthouse has been out of service since 1972; the beacon has sat on the high-rise ever since (focal height 114.7 m).

abschnitte.s: Is Travemünde home to Germany’s oldest lighthouse?
abschnitte.x: The Old Lighthouse of Travemünde (1539) is regarded as Germany’s oldest surviving lighthouse. As an active sea mark, however, it has been out of service since 1972.
From 1811 to 1813 Travemünde belonged to Napoleon’s French Empire. The “Fort Travemünde” was built at the estuary to enforce the Continental Blockade.
In 1889 the Hamburg merchants Wentzel and Dröge raced off Travemünde – the winner got a bottle of Lübeck Rotspon. It grew into one of the largest sailing events in the world.

abschnitte.t: Golf in Travemünde and the Bay of Lübeck
abschnitte.x: Right above the Brodten cliffs sits one of Germany’s oldest golf clubs – with two large courses within reach. What the courses are like, who may play and where to book.

abschnitte.t: Golf in Travemünde and the Bay of Lübeck
abschnitte.s: Which golf courses are there in Travemünde and the Bay of Lübeck?
abschnitte.x: Yes, you can play golf in Travemünde – at one of the most established courses on the German Baltic coast. The Lübeck-Travemünde Golf Club has sat high above the Brodten cliffs since 1921, with 27 holes and wide views over the Bay of Lübeck. For a golf holiday on the Baltic, the distances are short here: beach, promenade and golf course are all in the same town. Around Travemünde, the Bay of Lübeck adds two more large facilities – the Maritim Golfpark Ostsee near Warnsdorf with 33 holes and the Seeschlösschen course in Timmendorfer Strand with 36 holes. Together that is almost a hundred fairways within about fifteen minutes, from a championship course to a 6-hole short course for beginners. Guests with a DGV card are welcome at all three; book the green fee and tee time directly with each club.

abschnitte.s: Can you play golf in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Yes. The Lübeck-Travemünde Golf Club, founded in 1921, is right in Travemünde above the Brodten cliffs and offers 27 holes with views over the Baltic. Two more large facilities sit nearby.

abschnitte.t: Golf in Travemünde and the Bay of Lübeck

abschnitte.s: What is the golf season like in the Bay of Lübeck?
abschnitte.x: Play is year-round. The Lübeck-Travemünde club tiers its green fees by summer and winter greens, with the competition season running April to October. Current times and prices are on the club websites.

abschnitte.s: Can you play golf in Travemünde in winter?
abschnitte.x: Yes. The Lübeck-Travemünde Golf Club is open year-round and distinguishes summer and winter greens; outside the competition season (April–October) the course is often quieter. The Seeschlösschen driving range in Timmendorfer Strand has heated bays on two levels – for practice in winter too. Please check current opening hours and winter green fees with the club.

The small harbour away from the promenade: cutters, nets and boat sheds – here Travemünde still works on the water instead of marketing it. On the Baggersand, ten minutes’ walk from the Vorderreihe, lies the seaside resort’s other side: fishing boats on plain jetties, crab pots, halyards slapping in the wind. If you want harbour romance without staging, this is it. Right next door the sand sculptures fill the old boat halls – fishing harbour and exhibition make a natural pairing for a walk, especially in changeable weather. Handy for the day plan: Travemünde’s motorhome site lies right at the fishing harbour – no camper in town sleeps closer to the water (more on the camping page). And if the harbour walk leaves you hungry, the well-known fish-roll addresses are right here at the harbour and on the Vorderreihe – the food guide lists them with location and verification date. Local tip: Go in the morning: when the cutters come in, the harbour is Travemünde’s liveliest spot for half an hour.

A working harbour: respect the fishermen’s jetties and areas, keep children back from the edge. The sand sculpture exhibition is in the boat halls next door (Travemünder Landstraße 306). Fresh fish, if any, sells in the morning – there are no fixed sale hours. verified on 2 July 2026 All harbours at a glance →

abschnitte.x: Fresh fish, if any, is sold in the morning when the cutters come in – there are no fixed sale hours. It remains a working harbour, not a market.

abschnitte.x: The harbour walk with the sand sculpture exhibition in the boat halls next door – a natural pairing, especially in changeable weather.

The yacht harbour upriver: sheltered on the lower Trave, with boatyards next door and a short run towards the Pötenitzer Wiek. Where the Trave widens and calms down lies Marina Baltica – less shop window, more home port. For crews the position is practical: sheltered from the bay’s swell, with the big ships as neighbours on the way out to sea. By land it is a short hop into town; on the water, the quiet cruising ground of the Pötenitzer Wiek begins just beyond the marina. For getting there: the marina sits at Travemünder Landstraße 300, in the town’s south-west between the fishing harbour and Skandinavienkai – by water roughly one nautical mile upriver of the estuary, sheltered in a bay of the Trave. The operator runs it as a full-service harbour with boatyards next door; ask there directly for binding details on berths, crane and winter storage. Local tip: From the water, the evening run is the treat: down the Trave with the last light – the lit-up Vorderreihe appears right on cue.

Ask the operator directly about berths, crane and services. By train: the “Lübeck-Skandinavienkai” stop is closest. On the water: cross the big-ship fairway, do not linger in it. verified on 2 July 2026 All harbours at a glance →

abschnitte.x: Berths, crane and services are handled by the operator – binding information only from them. We deliberately do not quote invented berth or fee figures.

The berth right on the Vorderreihe: when a cruise ship calls at Travemünde, it moors here – in the middle of town, two minutes from the harbourside ice cream. Few Baltic resorts bring their cruise ships this close: at Ostpreußenkai the ship lies right on the promenade and guests step straight into town. For everyone else it works in reverse – a call day turns the Vorderreihe into a close-up ship viewing. Between calls the quay is simply the town centre’s best water view: ferries, fishing boats and the Passat across the Trave. Even without a cruise ship, Ostpreußenkai is one of the town centre’s best viewpoints: the Passat harbour and the Priwall lie opposite, the Priwall ferry shuttles to the left, and to the right the Trave opens into the Baltic. Benches along the Vorderreihe make it the most comfortable spot for ship watching – and the live map on the ships page shows what comes in next. Local tip: Evening departure is the moment: ship, low sun and the whole Vorderreihe waving – grab a spot on the Priwall side.

Ostpreußenkai is currently closed to ship calls while the quay wall’s stability is assessed. The only planned 2026 call (MS Europa) was cancelled; 2026 will likely pass without a cruise ship (as of July 2026). Best photo spots: the Priwall bank opposite (whole ship in frame) and the north pier for arrival/departure. On call days park early or take the train – the town centre fills up. verified on 2 July 2026 All harbours at a glance →
