abschnitte.x: Ostpreußenkai is a public quay right on the Vorderreihe – no fence. On call days arrive early or by train, the town centre fills up.

The marina under the Passat’s masts: leisure boats and visiting yachts on the Priwall side, with the best view back at the Vorderreihe. No Travemünde harbour has a bigger backdrop: the Passat’s four masts rise right above the jetties, the Priwall ferry crosses behind, and in the evening the Vorderreihe glows across the water. Arrive by boat and you moor in the middle of the picture. On foot the Passat harbour is part of the Priwall walk: ferry, museum ship, marina, beach – all in one line along the promenade. A few sourced numbers for context: the Passat harbour counts around 500 berths, making it the Priwall side’s main leisure-boat harbour. The Passat herself, built in 1911, has been moored above the harbour for decades. Right next door the Ostseestation shows local Baltic sea life in 20 display tanks – together with beach and nature reserve, a harbour visit easily grows into half a Priwall day. Local tip: Evening-light tip: from the jetties the whole Vorderreihe sits in the sun – the classic photo most visitors miss.

Berths and rates are handled by the operator – binding information only there. The Passat can be visited in season (see the leisure page). Arriving without a boat: Priwall ferry, then five minutes along the promenade. verified on 2 July 2026 All harbours at a glance →

Ferry port · Sweden and Finland · around the clock

Travemünde’s ferry port: the big ferries to Sweden and Finland leave from Skandinavienkai – trucks, cars and passengers, in any weather. Skandinavienkai sits upriver from the town centre – arriving by ferry you come ashore at Travemünde’s southern edge, not through the middle of it. Its own railway stop (“Lübeck-Skandinavienkai”) and the B75 connect the terminal; live train departures are on the getting-here page. The terminal itself is off limits to spectators – but the show belongs to everyone: arriving and departing ferries pass the estuary close to the north pier and the Priwall beach. The live ship map shows who is under way. The ferry trade shapes the whole town: with departures to Sweden and Finland spread around the clock, the big ships in the Trave estuary are part of everyday life – from the beach they feel close enough to touch. Planning a crossing yourself, you find the Finnlines routes (including Helsinki and Malmö) and TT-Line (Trelleborg) further down this page; train departures and traffic are gathered on the getting-here page. Local tip: The best “harbour tour” is free: stand on the north pier as a big ferry leaves – it swings into the fairway right in front of you.

Timetables and booking run directly via the operators – the route overview is on the getting-here page. Own railway stop with live departures; by car, follow the B75 signs. The terminal grounds are no viewpoint – watch from the north pier or the Priwall instead. verified on 2 July 2026 All harbours at a glance →

Founded 1187 · resort since 1802 · Lübeck since 1913

Travemünde was founded in 1187 at the mouth of the Trave and has belonged to Lübeck permanently since 1329. From a fortified border and customs post it grew, from 1802, into the second seaside resort on the German Baltic coast; in 1913 it lost its independence and became a district of Lübeck. This page tells the story in stages – with an interactive timeline from 1187 to today, each fact sourced.

abschnitte.s: Founding and the path to Lübeck (1187–1500)
abschnitte.x: Travemünde arose in 1187 at the strategically decisive mouth of the Trave – whoever controlled the estuary controlled the sea access to the rising trading city of Lübeck. In 1226 Lübeck secured rights to the place in an imperial charter of Frederick II, and the Priwall came to Travemünde. In 1329 Lübeck finally bought Travemünde; ever since, the town has been tied to the Hanseatic city.

abschnitte.s: Fortress, Napoleon and the rise of the resort (1500–1872)
abschnitte.x: As a fortified border and customs post, Travemünde guarded the estuary for centuries and repelled Danish attacks in 1510; in 1539 Dutch masons built the lighthouse that still stands. The fortifications were razed in 1807, and from 1811 to 1813 the town belonged to Napoleon’s French Empire. In parallel its rise as a spa began: as early as 1802 Travemünde had been recognised as the second seaside resort on the German Baltic coast.

With the railway from 1882, the Kaiser’s visit in 1894 and the 1.7-kilometre beach promenade (1898–1904), Travemünde became a fashionable resort. In 1911 the barque Passat was launched. In 1913 Travemünde was incorporated into Lübeck – and in the same period the Kurhaus, casino and Art Nouveau stations were built that still shape the townscape.

In 1933 the future chancellor Willy Brandt fled via Travemünde to Denmark. After 1945 the inner-German border ran right by the Priwall – the northernmost point of the Iron Curtain. Only in 1990 did that border fall, and the Priwall became freely accessible again. Since then Travemünde has kept changing: in 2004 the Old Lighthouse became a museum, in 2007 a cruise terminal was built, in 2012 the casino closed, and in 2020 the new Priwall promenade opened.

2012 The casino closes; the Kurhaus becomes a hotel. 2019 The Maritim high-rise, too, is listed as a monument. 2020 The new Priwall promenade opens. 2024 Travemünde has 13,903 inhabitants (as of 31 Dec). The tower of 1539 still stands today: it is considered Germany’s oldest lighthouse – its full story has its own page. verified on 1 July 2026
Travemünde was founded in 1187 – making it over 830 years old. The present Old Lighthouse dates from 1539.

abschnitte.s: Since when has Travemünde belonged to Lübeck?
abschnitte.x: Lübeck secured rights to Travemünde as early as 1226 and finally bought it in 1329. In 1913 Travemünde was incorporated into the Hanseatic city of Lübeck as a district.

abschnitte.s: Since when has Travemünde been a seaside resort?
abschnitte.x: Since 1802 – when Travemünde was recognised as the second seaside resort on the German Baltic coast and grew into a spa town.

abschnitte.s: Was Travemünde once its own town?
abschnitte.x: Yes. Travemünde was an independent town until its incorporation in 1913, and for centuries before that a fortified border and customs post at the mouth of the Trave.

abschnitte.s: Did the inner-German border run through Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Not through the town, but right by the Priwall: after 1945 the northernmost point of the inner-German border lay there. Only in 1990 did it fall – since 3 February 1990 the Priwall is freely accessible again.

abschnitte.s: Since when has Travemünde Week existed?
abschnitte.x: Since 1889: that year Hamburg merchants first held a sailing race off Travemünde, which grew into Travemünde Week.

abschnitte.s: What happened to Willy Brandt in Travemünde in 1933?
abschnitte.x: The future chancellor Willy Brandt fled via Travemünde by ship to Denmark in April 1933. A plaque in Jahrmarktstraße still recalls the escape.

abschnitte.s: Why was the Old Lighthouse switched off in 1972?
abschnitte.x: Because the new, 119-metre Maritim high-rise blocked the 31-metre tower’s view of the sea. In 1974 a beacon on the high-rise took over, with a focal height of 114.7 metres.

Pink, hearty and maritime: Labskaus – lapskaus in Scandinavia – is THE North German sailors’ dish. A mash of salted meat, potatoes and beetroot, crowned with a fried egg, rollmops and gherkin. What’s in it, where it comes from and why sailors of all people invented it – and what the people of Lübeck do differently.

Labskaus is a potato dish with salted beef and beetroot, common in North Germany, Scandinavia and – as “Scouse” – in Liverpool. Not a prettily arranged plate but a hearty, pink mash: everything is chopped and combined. The classic comes with crisp, sour sides that cut through the richness.

Salted beef or corned beef the savoury base – once preserved meat kept on board. Mashed potatoes bind everything into a loose purée. Beetroot gives the typical pink-red colour and a sweet-sour note. Onions sweated in lard or oil. Fried egg goes on top – part of the picture. Rollmops or matjes soused herring on the side, the contrast to the meat. Gherkin crisp and sour, often served with pickled beetroot. The arrangement is a matter of taste – classically the mash is topped with a fried egg, with rollmops, gherkin and beetroot alongside.

Labskaus is a true seafarers’ dish. It was first mentioned in 1706 by the English author Ned Ward as a sailors’ meal; an English-German dictionary of 1802 describes it as “a sailor’s dish of salted meat, biscuit and onions”. In German sources it appears in an 1878 nautical dictionary – with the potatoes already added. From the ports of the North and Baltic Seas it moved ashore: to Hamburg, Bremen, Lübeck, Flensburg and far into Scandinavia.

abschnitte.s: Why a mash of all things?
abschnitte.x: The reason is as practical as it is unappetising: on long voyages many sailors suffered from scurvy – a vitamin-C deficiency that loosened their teeth. Solid food was hard to chew. So everything was chopped and mashed. Beetroot and sour gherkins also provided vitamin C and helped prevent scurvy – long before anyone could explain the link.

The origin of the name is disputed – which is what makes it fun. Several readings circulate: from the English “lobscouse” (hence “Scouse”, the nickname for Liverpudlians); from Low German “Lappen” (a cut of belly meat) and “Kaus” (bowl); from a Norwegian sense of “something easy to chew”; and even from the Baltic “labs kauss” – “good bowl”. There is no single answer.

abschnitte.s: Regional variants – and the Lübeck exception
abschnitte.x: As simple as the base recipe is, the regions differ. Flensburg and North Frisia leave out the fish; elsewhere herring is a fixture. And Lübeck – of which Travemünde is part – has its own signature: here fish traditionally goes into the Labskaus. By the water, where the cutters land, that makes sense.

As a Baltic resort at the mouth of the Trave, Travemünde is exactly the kitchen Labskaus comes from: seafaring, harbour, fresh fish. Anyone wanting to try the maritime cuisine will find it at the fishing harbour and in the food guide – where you’ll also find the famous fish rolls . Labskaus isn’t on every menu, but it’s the hearty, honest classic of the region. verified on 10 July 2026 Source: Wikipedia “Labskaus” · recipe components and etymology
Classically: salted beef or corned beef, mashed potatoes, beetroot and onions, all combined. Plus a fried egg on top, and rollmops or matjes, gherkin and pickled beetroot on the side.
The colour comes from the beetroot mixed into the potato-and-meat mash. It gives the dish its characteristic pink-red hue and a slightly sweet-sour note.

abschnitte.s: Where does the name Labskaus come from?
abschnitte.x: The origin is disputed. Readings range from the English “lobscouse” (hence “Scouse” for Liverpool) to Low German “Lappen” (belly meat) and “Kaus” (bowl) to the Baltic “labs kauss” – “good bowl”.

abschnitte.s: Is Labskaus the same as lapskaus?
abschnitte.x: Yes – it’s the same dish. “Labskaus” is the North German spelling, “lapskaus” the Scandinavian one (Norway, Denmark, Sweden). In Liverpool a related version is called “Scouse”.
On long voyages scurvy (vitamin-C deficiency) loosened sailors’ teeth, making solid food hard to chew. Chopping and mashing everything was the answer – beetroot and gherkins also supplied vitamin C.

119 metres · landmark · heritage monument

Few buildings divide Travemünde like the Maritim: a 119-metre concrete tower from 1974 – to some an eyesore, to others the landmark itself. It carries Europe’s highest lighthouse, has been a protected monument since 2019 – and was once a deliberate signal in the Cold War. This page tells the story behind the silhouette.
119 m height (125 m with masts) 36 floors 1974 completed 114 m focal height of the lighthouse verified on 3 July 2026

abschnitte.s: A lighthouse of the Cold War
abschnitte.x: The Maritim was listed as a cultural monument by the city of Lübeck in July 2019 – and the justification tells the real story: the tower is not only striking in townscape terms but “a real and symbolic beacon of the free West”. It rose within sight of the inner-German border that ran across the eastern tip of the Priwall. When the GDR opened the modern Hotel Neptun in Warnemünde in 1971, the West answered with an even taller sign at the Trave estuary: the Maritim. A hotel tower became a political statement – system rivalry cast in concrete.

Since 1974 the Maritim has carried the sea light for the Travemünde harbour entrance – at 114 metres, regarded as Europe’s highest lighthouse. It took over from the Old Lighthouse of 1539, which had been retired two years earlier because the new tower literally blocked its view. So Travemünde has Germany’s oldest surviving lighthouse and its modern successor standing close together – an image that defines the town.

Not everyone finds the Maritim beautiful. To critics the concrete tower is a “1970s building sin”, an alien body above the resort; to others it is precisely the unmistakable landmark by which you recognise Travemünde from the train. Heritage conservation has settled the debate: the tower is worth protecting as a document of its time – including the 1970s-style interior. Since listing, every renovation has to be agreed with the heritage authority, which makes conversions more demanding.

The tower is more than a hotel: the lower floors house the Maritim Strandhotel, above them around 320 owner-occupied flats, plus shops, restaurants, an indoor pool and an underground garage. The view from the top is worth it – from the bar on the upper floors it reaches far across Lübeck Bay and the Priwall in clear weather.

abschnitte.s: How tall is the Maritim high-rise in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: The Maritim is 119 metres tall (125 metres with the radio masts on the roof) and has 36 floors. It was completed in 1974 and is Travemünde’s landmark.

abschnitte.s: Why is the Maritim a protected monument?
abschnitte.x: The city of Lübeck listed the tower in July 2019 – for its townscape value, its 1970s-style interior and because it counts as a “real and symbolic beacon of the free West” at the former zonal border.

abschnitte.s: What does the Maritim have to do with the GDR border?
abschnitte.x: The tower rose within sight of the inner-German border on the Priwall. When the GDR opened the Hotel Neptun in Warnemünde in 1971, the West answered with the even taller Maritim – a sign in the Cold War rivalry of systems.

abschnitte.s: Does the lighthouse really sit on the high-rise?
abschnitte.x: Yes. Since 1974 the Maritim has carried the sea light for the harbour entrance at 114 metres – regarded as Europe’s highest lighthouse. It replaced the Old Lighthouse of 1539, whose view the new building blocked.

abschnitte.s: Lights of the night – who flashes how?
abschnitte.x: Every navigational light has its own “character” – an unmistakable rhythm of light and dark by which seafarers recognise it at night. These are the lights of the Travemünde approach, with their real characters from the seamark data: Travemünde Fl Blitzfeuer mit roten und weißen Sektoren, alle 4 Sekunden The main approach light – since 1974 on the roof of the Maritim tower at 116 metres, Germany’s highest-mounted navigational light. Travemünde, N-Mole Oc unterbrochenes Feuer mit roten und grünen Sektoren, alle 4 Sekunden The main approach light – since 1974 on the roof of the Maritim tower at 116 metres, Germany’s highest-mounted navigational light. Priwall Oberfeuer Oc weißes unterbrochenes Feuer, 2 Unterbrechungen alle 9 Sekunden Leading-light pair on the Priwall: keep both lights in line and you are exactly in the fairway. Priwall Unterfeuer Oc weißes unterbrochenes Feuer, 2 Unterbrechungen alle 9 Sekunden The lower partner of the leading-light pair. Oberfeuer Siechenbucht Oc weißes unterbrochenes Feuer, alle 4 Sekunden Second leading-light pair for the inner Trave bend at the Siechenbucht. Unterfeuer Siechenbucht Oc weißes unterbrochenes Feuer, alle 4 Sekunden The lower partner at the Siechenbucht. And the Old Lighthouse? It has been dark since 1974: when the Maritim tower blocked its view, its light moved to the tower’s roof.

Every number on this site should be traceable: what is measured, how often, from which source – and what cannot be concluded from it.

Travemünde heute is an independent project by Christian Fizia from Travemünde – not an official site of the city of Lübeck or the resort administration. Its purpose is simple: to gather the information about Travemünde that is scattered across many portals in one place – with open sources, a visible verification date and this traceable methodology. The site is growing in scope; full operator details are in the imprint.

For listed venues, the publicly visible overall rating and the number of reviews are retrieved once a day via the official Google API. Only these two numbers plus the date are stored. Review texts or author names are never stored. These numbers form the history. If the number of visible reviews drops, that is shown – without any statement about the cause. Reviews disappear for many reasons: Google removes detected fakes automatically (over 240 million in 2024 alone), authors delete their own posts, accounts are closed, or businesses have inadmissible reviews checked. Which reason applies in a given case cannot be determined from outside – and is therefore not claimed here. The displayed values are documented observations, not a rating of the venue by this site. The observation start date is shown on every history; there is no retroactive data. Illustrative chart with invented numbers – not real data.

The directory combines two sources: structure, location and opening hours come from OpenStreetMap (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0); photos, descriptions and rating values from the public Google Maps listings. Photo rights remain with their authors; every rating links its Google Maps listing as the source. Details can age – when in doubt, the linked website of the place counts.

Weather and water temperature come from Open-Meteo, the water level from the official Travemünde gauge (Pegelonline/WSV), the bathing water status from Schleswig-Holstein open data (official laboratory samples, roughly monthly in season – not a live reading). Every value carries its source and timestamp.

Posts in the social overview are gathered automatically – no fixed account list: from Mastodon via its open API (hashtags #travemuende and #travemünde), from Instagram once a day via a scraping service (hashtag #travemuende). Each tile shows a short text excerpt and a downscaled preview image stored on our server, and links to the original. Content and rights remain with their authors.
Events are maintained editorially; every entry states its source and the date of its last verification. Overdue entries are visibly marked rather than hidden.

The day planner selects exclusively from this site’s verified place database – it cannot invent destinations. Composition runs rule-based in the browser: interests, season, weekday and the weather forecast filter the candidates, then a schedule is built without overlaps and with buffer time. Walking times are marked as estimates (straight line with a detour factor), not navigation routes. Inputs are not sent to any server; the last plan lives only in your own browser.

Lighthouse · Seebadmuseum · Passat · sand sculptures

Travemünde has four museums and exhibitions worth seeing – and each shows the town from a different angle: technology and a view in the Old Lighthouse, local history in the Seebadmuseum, the world of cargo sailers on the Passat, and huge sand art at the fishing harbour. This page sorts out what is worth what.

Germany’s oldest surviving lighthouse (1539) shows the history of lighthouse technology across eight storeys. 142 steps lead up to the roughly 30-metre gallery with a view over the old town, the Passat and the Bay of Lübeck. In the historic Gesellschaftshaus, the Seebadmuseum tells Travemünde’s history across 160 m² – from fortified border post to imperial summer resort to the border history at the Priwall, with films, photos, audio stations and exhibits. abschnitte.t: Words you only hear in the North
abschnitte.x: You hear it the moment you reach the Baltic: the North’s own way of speaking. A “Moin” at any time of day, “Schietwetter” when it pours, and a “Klönschnack” by the harbour. Here are the finest North German and Low German words – briefly explained, so you can join in the chat in Travemünde.

abschnitte.t: Words you only hear in the North
abschnitte.x: Moin The Northern greeting – used at ANY time of day, not just in the morning. In use: “Moin!” – even at 3 pm. Moin Moin The doubled version. To some Northerners it already counts as chatter – one “Moin” is plenty. Schietwetter Bad, cold, wet weather. “Schiet” means muck – so the weather is rubbish. In use: “In this Schietwetter we’re staying in.” Schmuddelwetter Grey, damp, dreary – the quieter cousin of Schietwetter. Klönschnack A cosy, relaxed chat – often over the garden fence or at the harbour. In use: “We had a little Klönschnack.” schnacken to talk, to chat. “Platt schnacken” means to speak Low German. Deern A girl or young woman – always affectionate, never derogatory. In use: “Well, my Deern?” Jung / Jung' A boy or young lad – the male counterpart to Deern. Feudel The floor cloth. “feudeln” = to mop the floor. In use: “I still need to feudeln.” Buddel A bottle. A “Buddelschiff” is a ship in a bottle. Lütt little. A “Lütt un Lütt” is a small beer with a schnapps. In use: “A little one, please.” Fofftein A break – literally “fifteen” (minutes). “Fofftein maken” = to take a break. tüddelig / vertüddelt confused, muddled. To get “vertüddelt” is to get tangled up. In use: “I’m all in a muddle.” Puschen Slippers. sabbeln to chatter, to prattle. “Sabbel” can also mean the mouth. dröge dry – of the weather and of humour (“dröger Humor”).

abschnitte.t: Words you only hear in the North
abschnitte.x: Muckefuck Weak or ersatz coffee – the “Plörre” of hot drinks. Plörre A weak, watery drink – usually bad coffee. betüddeln / betütern to fuss over someone, to coddle. nölen to whine, grumble, dawdle. Kladderadatsch a big mess, chaos – often with a crash. angeschickert tipsy, slightly drunk. kabbelig Of the sea: choppy, short steep waves – a “kabbelige See”. achtern at the back. Nautical: “nach achtern” = towards the stern. Steert the (rear) end, the tail – in sailors’ talk also a rope’s end. pütschern to potter about, or to splash around in the water. Nordlicht Jokingly: a Northern German – not only the aurora. Hummel Hummel A Hamburg call; the correct reply is “Mors Mors”. Known with a wink around the Baltic too. verified on 10 July 2026 Source: common North German and Low German usage (regional)

abschnitte.t: Words you only hear in the North
abschnitte.x: “Moin” is the North German greeting – used at any time of day, not just in the morning. It probably comes from “moi” (nice/good), not from “Morgen” (morning).

abschnitte.s: Is “Moin” only said in the morning?
abschnitte.x: No. “Moin” works all day – morning, noon and night. That’s exactly what surprises newcomers.

abschnitte.x: Plattdeutsch (Low German) is the traditional regional language of North Germany. Many everyday words like “schnacken”, “Deern” or “Feudel” come from it.

Germany’s oldest lighthouse · 1330 · 31 metres

The old lighthouse in Travemünde is the oldest lighthouse in Germany. Its history reaches back to the 14th century: from the first documentary mention in 1330 through the rebuilding of 1539 to the brick tower of 1827, which is a maritime museum today.

A lighthouse – Latin lucerna – in Travemünde is first documented in 1330. That makes it the oldest lighthouse in Germany. Its history as a sea mark at the mouth of the Trave thus reaches back to the 14th century.

In 1534 Danish troops destroyed the tower during the Count’s Feud. The present structure was built in 1539 by Dutch bricklayers and has stood on the coast of the Bay of Lübeck for almost five centuries.

In its present classicist form of red brick the tower was built in 1827. It stands 31 metres tall and still shapes the silhouette of the seafront. The red brick gave the lighthouse its unmistakable face.

After almost 450 years in service the lighthouse was switched off in 1972: the new Maritim high-rise blocked the view and took over the task of guiding ships with the highest lighthouse beacon in Europe. Read more about the Maritim and its beacon in its own chapter.

Since 2004 the tower has been a maritime museum of lighthouse technology. From the 31-metre platform the view reaches far across the mouth of the Trave. More on the town’s history under History . verified on 10 July 2026 Source: Wikipedia “Leuchtturm Travemünde” · travemuende-tourismus.de · luebeck.de
Germany’s oldest lighthouse stands in Travemünde, the Baltic resort at the mouth of the Trave that belongs to Lübeck. The old lighthouse shapes the seafront there.

abschnitte.s: How old is the old lighthouse in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: The present structure dates from 1539. A lighthouse on this spot is first documented as early as 1330, which is why it is regarded as the oldest lighthouse in Germany.

abschnitte.s: Why was the lighthouse switched off in 1972?
abschnitte.x: The neighbouring Maritim high-rise blocked the view of the old beacon. In 1972 it took over the task of guiding ships with the highest lighthouse beacon in Europe.

abschnitte.s: How tall is the old lighthouse?
abschnitte.x: The old lighthouse in Travemünde is 31 metres tall. It was built in its present form of red brick in 1827.
Yes. Since 2004 the tower has been a maritime museum of lighthouse technology and also a viewing tower. From the platform 31 metres up the view reaches across the mouth of the Trave.

abschnitte.t: Opening hours and Sunday shopping in Travemünde
abschnitte.x: In Travemünde you can shop on Sundays thanks to the “Bäderregelung” (spa rule): in season – 15 March to 31 October and around Christmas/New Year (17 December to 8 January) – shops may open on Sundays and public holidays for six hours between 11 am and 7 pm. This page explains simply when and where you can shop.

abschnitte.t: Opening hours and Sunday shopping in Travemünde
abschnitte.x: Yes, Sunday shopping is possible in Travemünde – as a seaside resort it is covered by the spa rule. Six hours are allowed within the 11 am–7 pm window; each shop sets its exact times itself. Only in season: 15 March–31 October and 17 December–8 January. Otherwise Sundays stay closed. Everyday and tourist goods may be sold – not everything is allowed.

abschnitte.t: Opening hours and Sunday shopping in Travemünde
abschnitte.x: In Germany shops are generally closed on Sundays. Schleswig-Holstein, however, allows recognised holiday and spa towns an exception – the “Bäderregelung” (spa regulation). As a seaside resort, Travemünde is included. In season, shops may open on Sundays and holidays for six hours within the 11 am–7 pm window and sell everyday and tourist goods. The rule currently applies until 2028.

abschnitte.t: Opening hours and Sunday shopping in Travemünde
abschnitte.x: Monday to Saturday Largely unrestricted by law. Most shops open around 9 am–6 pm, larger ones until 8 pm. Sunday/holiday in season 15 March–31 October and 17 December–8 January: opening allowed, six hours within 11 am–7 pm. Easter Sunday Special rule: 2:00 pm to 6:30 pm. Sunday/holiday off-season 1 November–14 December and 9 January–14 March: shops stay closed on Sundays. Excluded all year Good Friday and Christmas Day; on 1 May a restriction applies. The legal basis is the Schleswig-Holstein “Bäderverordnung”, which allows spa and resort towns like Travemünde to open on Sundays (sources: schleswig-holstein.de, IHK Schleswig-Holstein). verified on 1 July 2026

Parking costs vary in Travemünde depending on location – new fees have applied since 1 June 2025. It is most expensive near the beach, and free at the edge of town. This page summarises the current zones and prices, shows the large free car park at Kowitzberg and explains the rules for motorhomes and EVs – with source and verification date so the figures are right.

abschnitte.s: What does parking cost in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Fees depend on the parking zone. Central, beach-side spaces (Mövenstein, Leuchtenfeld, ferry harbour) are in the more expensive Zone IV, edge areas in Zone V. Charges apply daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Zone IV (central: Mövenstein, Leuchtenfeld, ferry harbour) 30 min 1,60 € · up to 3,20 €/h · day ticket 12 € Zone V (edge area) 30 min 1,20 € · no day ticket Fees since 1 June 2025 (Hansestadt Lübeck / KWL). Peninsula at the Trave estuary · by ferry

The Priwall is the roughly three-kilometre peninsula opposite the town centre, separated only by the Trave and reached by ferry in a few minutes. Here you find the broad, quieter sandy beach, the museum ship Passat with the Passat harbour, the marine station and a large nature reserve – and until 1990 the inner-German border ran across its eastern tip. This page brings together what defines the Priwall, with source and verification date.

The broad sandy beach on the north-east of the peninsula is the quieter, more spacious one in Travemünde – with beach chairs, naturist and dog-beach sections. Opposite lies the busier Kurstrand. The visitor tax also applies on the Priwall . Beach and water → Landmark

Built in 1911, the tall ship is permanently moored at the Passat harbour on the Priwall and open as a museum ship – one of the last of its kind. The harbour offers around 500 berths. What a four-masted barque actually is . Ships and Passat → Sailing
The Priwall side’s leisure-boat harbour lies right under the Passat’s masts – around 500 berths and visiting yachts, with the best view back at the Vorderreihe. Passat harbour page → With children

Baltic aquarium and marine museum right at the Passat harbour: 20 display tanks with local sea creatures, touch pools, net excursions and microscopy courses. Run by the non-profit “Natur und Umwelt – Ostseestation Travemünde e. V.”, open year-round. ostseestation-travemuende.de ↗ Market and food
The market hall gathers delicatessen, regional souvenirs and dining under one roof – a worthwhile stop right after the ferry. Shopping → Nature

The southern half of the peninsula has been a nature reserve since 1998 (around 150 hectares) with dunes, salt meadows and the Pötenitz bay – a quiet contrast to the beach bustle. Day trips → verified on 1 July 2026

abschnitte.s: The border straight across the Priwall
abschnitte.x: The state border with Mecklenburg-Vorpommern runs across the eastern tip of the Priwall – until 1990 this was the inner-German border between the Federal Republic and the GDR. The peninsula has belonged to Lübeck-Travemünde since incorporation in 1913; today around 1,600 people live permanently on the Priwall, plus some 400 summer-house guests. Where the fence once stood, a path now follows the old border. More on the division and reunification is on the history page. To the history of Travemünde and the division →

Priwall-East is a year-round dog beach – the main beach is closed to dogs in summer. With a dog → Beach chairs are available at the Priwall beach too – rentals with contact in the guide. Beach chairs → Boats and SUP: the Passat harbour marina and the rentals in town are a few minutes away. Boat rental and party boats → Food: the Fischerkajüte on the Priwall and the BeachBay market hall. Food and fish rolls → Right by the ferry landing sits Moin’sen im Fährhaus – regional cuisine with a view of the Trave, dogs welcome. Moin’sen im Fährhaus → Staying on the peninsula: Strandcamping Priwall (since 1958) and a motorhome pitch near the beach. Camping and motorhomes → Holiday flat or hotel? Which location suits which stay is covered by the accommodation guide. Accommodation →

abschnitte.s: The Priwall in 1878 – racecourse, not border
abschnitte.x: On the official 1878 sheet the Priwall is almost empty – it records a racecourse and the Vorderreihe ferry. Of the inner-German border that ran here from 1945 to 1990 the map knows nothing. The slider compares the Pötenitz Wiek of that time with today’s aerial image. abschnitte.s: How do you get to the Priwall?
abschnitte.x: Across the Trave by the Priwall ferry: a car ferry takes vehicles over, a year-round passenger and bicycle ferry brings pedestrians and cyclists across in a few minutes. From the town centre (Vorderreihe) it is only a few steps to the landing.

abschnitte.s: What can you do on the Priwall?
abschnitte.x: Swim at the broad sandy beach, visit the museum ship Passat, see the Passat harbour with its marina, visit the marine station with its aquariums, stop at the BeachBay market hall and walk in the nature reserve on the southern half.

abschnitte.s: Is the Priwall beach better than the Kurstrand?
abschnitte.x: Different: the Priwall beach is the broader, quieter beach with more space, while the Kurstrand in the town centre is busier and closer to the promenade. Both are officially designated bathing sites.

abschnitte.s: Did the inner-German border really run across the Priwall?
abschnitte.x: Yes. The eastern tip of the Priwall forms the border with Mecklenburg-Vorpommern; until 1990 this was the border between the Federal Republic and the GDR. The peninsula itself belonged to the Federal Republic (Lübeck).

A Baltic aquarium and marine museum at the Passat harbour with 20 display tanks of local sea life, touch pools and excursions, run by the non-profit “Natur und Umwelt – Ostseestation Travemünde e. V.”. Open year-round (mind the seasonal hours).
Across the Trave to the Priwall · Stadtwerke Lübeck

The Priwall ferry links the Vorderreihe in the town centre with the Priwall peninsula – for passengers and cars, year-round and at short intervals during the day. The crossing over the Trave takes only a few minutes. This page answers the most common questions: what the ferry costs in 2026, when it runs and who travels free – with the current disruption status and a link to the operator’s binding timetable.

abschnitte.s: Where does the Priwall ferry run?
abschnitte.x: Car ferry: Vorderreihe ↔ Priwall The short crossing in the town centre – for cars, bikes and passengers, about five minutes. Across lie the Passat and the Priwall beach . Passenger ferry: Nordermole ↔ Priwall The second, more northerly line at the Nordermole – passengers and bikes only, no cars. It runs year-round with seasonal hours (until 10:30 p.m. in summer, 8 p.m. in winter); the return from the Priwall leaves immediately after arrival. Map geometry: OpenStreetMap (ODbL).

Priwall residents with their main residence on the peninsula cross free of charge, as does hand luggage (bags, cases, folding bikes). Everyone else pays the tariff. Regular commuters travel far more cheaply with a weekly, monthly or annual pass than with single tickets. Arriving by car? Find parking and petrol stations in town beforehand.

Priwall ferry (Stadtwerke Lübeck) The main car and passenger ferry from the Vorderreihe – year-round, at short intervals. Norderfähre A separate passenger ferry for pedestrians and cyclists a little further north at the Nordermole – year-round, with seasonal operating hours (shorter in winter). By car without the ferry Only via the long land route through Mecklenburg (eastern side, towards Boltenhagen/Rostock, via the A20) – impractical for a short visit.

abschnitte.s: What does the Priwall ferry cost in 2026?
abschnitte.x: A single crossing costs 2,10 € per person and 5,10 € for a car up to 3.5 t, a bicycle 1,20 € (as of 1 January 2026, Stadtwerke Lübeck). Frequent travellers save with multi-trip, weekly, monthly or annual passes.

abschnitte.s: Who travels on the Priwall ferry for free?
abschnitte.x: Priwall residents with their main residence on the peninsula travel free, as does hand luggage (bags, cases, folding bikes). Everyone else pays the tariff.

abschnitte.s: When does the Priwall ferry run?
abschnitte.x: The car ferry runs around the clock, 365 days a year: during the day (about 5 a.m. to 10:45 p.m.) it shuttles every 10 to 15 minutes; at night it departs Travemünde on a fixed schedule – every quarter-hour from 11 p.m. to midnight and 3 to 4 a.m., every half-hour from midnight to 2 a.m.; from the Priwall it returns immediately after arrival. Special timetables – e.g. during Travemünde Week – are on the operator’s timetable page (as of 18 July 2026).

abschnitte.s: Does the Priwall ferry run at night?
abschnitte.x: Yes. The car ferry also runs through the night – every half-hour between midnight and 2 a.m. (at minute 00 and 30 from Travemünde), every quarter-hour between 11 p.m. and midnight and between 3 and 4 a.m. The separate Nordermole passenger ferry, by contrast, keeps fixed seasonal hours and does not run at night (except for extended times during Travemünde Week and on New Year’s Eve).

abschnitte.s: How long is the crossing to the Priwall?
abschnitte.x: Only a few minutes – the Trave is narrow here. From the Vorderreihe landing to the Priwall takes barely longer than boarding and disembarking.

abschnitte.s: Can you reach the Priwall by car without the ferry?
abschnitte.x: Only via the long land route through Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (eastern side, via the A20). For visitors from Travemünde the ferry is the only practical way. There is no tunnel to the Priwall.

abschnitte.s: Can you buy the ferry ticket online or by app?
abschnitte.x: You pay on board; season tickets and passes are available from Stadtwerke Lübeck. Whether a single ticket can be bought online or via an app is best checked directly with Stadtwerke Lübeck (swhl.de).

On the Priwall, on the Priwall promenade right by the water
Ahoi is the casual fish and seafood concept of TV chef Steffen Henssler on the Priwall promenade, right by the water with a view of the Baltic.

On the Priwall promenade, where large fishing boats enter the Bay of Lübeck, the Ahoi menu ranges from fish and chips to sushi bowls, tuna sashimi and shrimp dishes and currywurst – under the motto “The main thing is tasty!”. It is the second Ahoi location and sits right by the water. Online ordering and reservation are possible, and dogs are welcome. The TA.SH tourism data name the Hamburg brothers Steffen and Peter Henssler as the operators, who opened the Ahoi in Travemünde in 2019, and list German classics such as currywurst and schnitzel Henssler style alongside sushi bowls and fish and chips. The large outdoor terrace sits where the Trave flows into the Bay of Lübeck. The address belongs to the Priwall – from the town centre the way leads across the Priwall ferry or the long way round via Mecklenburger Landstraße.

An entrance with an archway and flowers, several indoor rooms over two floors and an outdoor area with wooden tables and a fountain shape the ambience. The house is run by Marco Ceccaroli and his team; food is also available to take away. On the cliff, high above the Bay of Lübeck
Café Hermannshöhe is a self-service café with a panoramic view, set high above the Bay of Lübeck on the Travemünde cliff.

High above the sea on the cliff in the protected landscape between Travemünde and Niendorf, the Hermannshöhe serves breakfast, home-made cakes from its own bakery and changing lunch dishes including fish and North-German classics. The self-service format keeps prices moderate and waits short. Families find an outdoor area with a playground; in the evening the house serves as an event venue. The TA.SH tourism data describe the kitchen as traditional Holstein cooking with fish dishes and North-German classics. The opening details differ between sources: the website gives 11 am to 7 pm daily, OpenStreetMap lists seasonal hours with an earlier start at weekends – worth checking the website before setting out. It is the only address in this guide outside the town itself, a good three kilometres north of the beach promenade on top of the cliff; on foot the way leads along the shore path towards Niendorf.

On the Priwall, right by the Travemünde fishing harbour
Ristorante CasaGrande sits right by the Travemünde fishing harbour on the Priwall and offers Italian cuisine with regional fish and seafood.

From the CasaGrande you look out freely over the harbour scene and the Priwall. The cuisine is Italian with fine specialities, regional fish and seafood dishes and selected wines; lamb fillet is among the dishes mentioned. The restaurant also suits business dinners and family celebrations according to its own description. The TA.SH tourism data list the CasaGrande as an Italian restaurant right at the fishing harbour and highlight the glass frontage, the terrace and the wine selection. The fishing harbour at Baggersand is the working harbour of the town: the cutters set out from here and their catch is sold in Travemünde – at this address the short way from quay to kitchen is geography rather than a figure of speech. Tuesday is the closing day; on the other days, according to the website, service runs from midday through to the evening.

In the historic Alte Vogtei on the Vorderreihe, opposite the Priwall ferry
Fisch und Meer “in der Alten Vogtei” is a family-run restaurant and café in a historic building on the Vorderreihe, opposite the Priwall ferry.

The house describes itself as “modern cuisine in historic dress” and, since mid-2014, uses various areas of the Alte Vogtei with indoor and outdoor seating, each with its own charm. It offers a varied, regularly changing selection of fish dishes, meals, cakes and drinks. Reservations are also possible via WhatsApp. The TA.SH tourism data list pasta, meat dishes and cakes alongside fish and highlight the regularly changing menu as well as freshly caught fish from the nearby Baltic. The Alte Vogtei at Vorderreihe 7 is one of the historic houses in the old town; the restaurant uses several areas inside it. Luzifer sits at Baggersand on the Trave, a few steps from the Priwall ferry, and focuses on regional, seasonal “coastal cuisine” with its own coffee, baked goods and beer.

Through the glazed front and the two-storey terrace you look out over the Trave and the harbour with its ferries and cruise ships. The house makes its own coffee, espresso, baked goods and ASGAARD beer and, besides the à-la-carte menu, offers a brunch and a breakfast buffet on Sundays. The upper deck seats up to 100 people and is used for celebrations and company events. Baggersand is the street at the fishing harbour: the Travemünde cutters set out from here, and the fish sales and the motorhome park are right next door. The Priwall ferry pier is a few steps away, so the terrace looks out on the working Trave – ferries, cutters and the cruise ships at the quay opposite. On the operating status: the restaurant’s own website reports a temporary closure due to water damage as of 5 September 2026; the house is currently not listed in the TA.SH tourism data either. Sights · lighthouse · Passat · Brodten cliffs

Travemünde can be walked in a day – the main sights all sit between the beach, the Trave bank and the Priwall: the Old Lighthouse, the four-masted barque Passat, the Vorderreihe and the Brodten cliffs, with the Priwall just minutes away by ferry. The context comes from this page; the data on every place from the directory. Coast planner: Turn these points into a day programme in 30 seconds – with times, walking estimates and a map.
The landmark where the Vorderreihe meets the beach promenade: the brick tower with the Maritim high-rise as its unequal neighbour – the most photographed motif in town. Best in evening light.
The tall ship on the Priwall bank is visible across the Trave from the Vorderreihe and a few minutes away by ferry. Open as a museum ship in season; the masts alone are worth the crossing.
The peninsula opposite the town centre: promenade and marina at the front, quiet nature behind – natural beach, dunes and the view back to Travemünde. The ferry ride is part of the experience.
The waterfront mile: arriving ferries almost within reach, gabled houses and restaurants behind, and in season the sand sculpture exhibition. The liveliest spot in town at night.

North of the Kurstrand the coast rises into cliffs – the path on top runs towards Niendorf with wide views across the Bay of Lübeck. Sturdy shoes; no bathing at the natural shore below. Beach sections and water in detail → verified on 10 June 2026

abschnitte.s: What are the sights in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: The main fixed points are the Old Lighthouse on the beach promenade, the four-masted barque Passat on the Priwall bank, the Vorderreihe with its gabled houses and arriving ferries, the Priwall with its natural beach and marina, and the Brodten cliffs north of the Kurstrand. In total the directory records 49 sights with photos and a map.

abschnitte.s: Can you visit the Old Lighthouse in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: The Old Lighthouse can be seen from outside at any time – it stands where the Vorderreihe meets the beach promenade and is the most photographed motif in town, especially in evening light.

abschnitte.s: What can you see in Travemünde in a day?
abschnitte.x: The five main points – lighthouse, Vorderreihe, Priwall with the Passat (by ferry), beach promenade and Brodten cliffs – are all within walking distance and can be experienced in a day. The coast planner turns them into a day programme in 30 seconds.

abschnitte.s: How do you get to the four-masted barque Passat?
abschnitte.x: The Passat lies on the Priwall bank of the Trave and is visible from the Vorderreihe. It is a few minutes away by the Priwall ferry; the museum ship can be visited in season.

The big ferries sail right through the town, cruise ships moor along the promenade, and the four-masted barque Passat lies as a museum ship on the Priwall – ship spotting is everyday life in Travemünde. abschnitte.s: Where is the best place to watch ships in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Closest is the Nordermole and the promenade, where the ferries pass within a few metres. The Priwall side is calmer, and the Brodten cliffs offer an elevated view.

abschnitte.s: Do cruise ships call at Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Yes, but rarely. Cruise ships moor at the Ostpreußenkai right on the promenade; confirmed calls are listed above on this page.

abschnitte.s: Can I see live which ships are around?
abschnitte.x: Yes – the live map on this page shows current ship positions on the Trave and in the Bay of Lübeck after a click.

abschnitte.s: What is the Passat in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: The Passat is a four-masted barque and one of the last surviving cargo sailing ships in the world. She lies as a museum ship at the Passat harbour on the Priwall side and is easy to see from the Vorderreihe.

abschnitte.s: Is there a sea-rescue station in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Yes – the DGzRS is stationed in Travemünde, with the rescue boat “Erich Koschubs”. More on the sea-rescue page.
Vorderreihe by the harbour · owner-run · no malls

Shopping in Travemünde means above all the Vorderreihe – the promenade street right by the harbour, lined with small, owner-run shops: maritime fashion, handmade jewellery, an independent bookshop and delicatessen. The big malls and outlets are in Lübeck and around; this page deliberately lists only the fine addresses in town – curated, with source and verification date.

At the fishing harbour on the Baggersand the fishermen sell the fresh catch – if at all, in the morning and without fixed hours. More on the harbour page.

The Vorderreihe is the shopping and strolling street right by the harbour; a few steps behind lies the quieter Kurgartenstraße with more small shops. As a seaside resort, many shops also open on Sundays in season – exact hours vary by shop, so check ahead if in doubt. The large malls and outlets (LUV Shopping, CITTI-PARK, Designer Outlet) are in Lübeck and Neumünster – not in Travemünde. This page deliberately focuses on the owner-run addresses in town. abschnitte.s: Where can you shop in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: The main shopping street is the Vorderreihe right by the harbour, with the Kurgartenstraße behind it. There you find small, owner-run shops for maritime fashion, jewellery, books and gifts. There is no large mall in town – those are in Lübeck.

abschnitte.s: Are there owner-run shops in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Yes, several – including the bookshop BuchANKER (Vorderreihe 1), the fashion house DRESS UP/Matzen (Vorderreihe 58 and 63), the maritime shop Seaside No. 64 (Vorderreihe 55) and MareSchmuck with handmade jewellery (Kurgartenstraße 17).

abschnitte.s: Is there a shopping mall or outlet in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Not in town. The large malls (LUV Shopping, CITTI-PARK) are in Lübeck, the Designer Outlet is in Neumünster. Travemünde itself stands out for small, owner-run shops on the Vorderreihe.

abschnitte.s: Are shops in Travemünde open on Sundays?
abschnitte.x: As a seaside resort, many shops also open on Sundays in season. Exact hours differ by shop – when in doubt, check the respective shop’s page in advance.

abschnitte.s: Where can I get Lübeck marzipan in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: The original (Niederegger) comes from Lübeck; in Travemünde delicatessens and souvenir shops carry it, e.g. on the Vorderreihe and in the BeachBay market hall on the Priwall. We only list a dedicated marzipan maker in town if it is verified.

Travemünde has no municipal indoor pool of its own – but the Baltic Sea on the doorstep and a publicly accessible spa with pools. Anyone wanting to swim in a pool finds the best option at the aja SEEBAD, which also admits day guests; the nearest public indoor pools are in Lübeck. This page sorts the options honestly – from the warm pool to a plunge into the Baltic.

Prussian land survey 1878 ↔ aerial image today

Three views, one handle: the official sheets of the Prussian land survey of 1878–1880 lie here in register over today's official aerial image. At the Brodten cliff this makes visible what is otherwise just a number: at 50 to 100 centimetres of retreat per year, the 1878 shoreline now lies a calculated 74 to 148 metres out – in the water. Drag the slider (or use the arrow keys) to switch between 1878 and today.

abschnitte.s: Town centre and Priwall: the seaside resort of 1878
abschnitte.x: The 1878 sheet already shows the ferry at the Vorderreihe – exactly where the Priwall ferry departs to this day – plus a “Seebad” and “Seepavillon” on the beach and a “Rennbahn” (racecourse) on the Priwall. The comparison with the aerial image shows how the resort grew around promenade and spa quarter, while the street grid of the Vorderreihe has stayed the same for almost 150 years. Comparison Town centre and Priwall: the seaside resort of 1878: position between 1878 (left) and today (right)

abschnitte.s: Brodten cliff: the 1878 coast now lies in the water
abschnitte.x: The Brodten cliff retreats 50 to 100 centimetres a year. Since the 1878 survey that adds up to a calculated 74 to 148 metres: the shoreline drawn on the old sheet now lies far out in the Bay of Lübeck. The slider makes this coast's strongest force visible – the abrasion that moves the cliff inland year after year, feeding the beaches of the neighbouring resorts with sand. Comparison Brodten cliff: the 1878 coast now lies in the water: position between 1878 (left) and today (right)

abschnitte.s: Pötenitz Wiek: where the border later ran
abschnitte.x: On the 1878 sheet the Pötenitz Wiek is simply a quiet bay between the Priwall and the Mecklenburg shore. Only the 20th century wrote history here: from 1945 to 1990 the inner-German border ran along the Priwall’s eastern tip – the beach ended at the fence. Today the tip is a nature reserve, and the Wiek again belongs to sailors and sea eagles. abschnitte.s: What did Travemünde look like around 1880?
abschnitte.x: The Prussian land survey of 1878–1880 shows a compact seaside resort: the Vorderreihe with the ferry to the Priwall, sea baths and a sea pavilion on the beach, a racecourse on the otherwise almost empty Priwall – and much open land where promenade and spa quarter stand today. The slider on this page lays the sheet directly over today’s aerial image.

abschnitte.s: How much land has the Brodten cliff lost since 1878?
abschnitte.x: At the documented 50 to 100 centimetres of retreat per year, the survey of 1878 gives a calculated 74 to 148 metres. It is a calculated range from the long-term retreat rate, not a single measurement – the map comparison makes the scale visible.

abschnitte.s: Where do the old maps come from and may they be used?
abschnitte.x: The sheets come from the Prussian land survey (Chronologen map series 1878–1950) of Schleswig-Holstein’s state survey office and are licensed CC BY 4.0 – free to use with attribution. The present-day comparison image is the official DOP20 orthophoto from the open geodata.

Travemünde’s visitor’s tax is officially the spa levy (Kurabgabe): overnight guests pay 3.50 € per person per day in the high season (15 May to 14 September) and 2.00 € in the low season. Day visitors pay a beach fee of 3.50 € – 2.00 € after 3 p.m. – in the high season only. Lübeck residents and children are exempt. This page answers the detailed questions, backed by the Hansestadt Lübeck by-law. Today (low season): overnight stay 2.00 € per person per day · the beach is free for day visitors. High season 15 May to 14 September: 3.50 €, beach fee 3.50 € (2.00 € after 3 p.m.).

Per person and overnight stay, adults from 18. The arrival day is not charged (§ 7 of the by-law) – you pay per night, usually via the host (hotel, holiday flat). abschnitte.s: Who is exempt? Lübeck residents, children, disabled visitors
abschnitte.x: The Hansestadt Lübeck by-law sets out the exemptions conclusively – these are the most important: Lübeck residents Exempt – anyone whose habitual residence or main residence is in the Hansestadt Lübeck pays neither the spa levy nor the beach fee (§ 5 (1) no. 7, § 14 d). Children and young people Spa levy free up to the age of 18 (proof of age); beach fee free up to the age of 16 (§ 5 (1) no. 1, § 14 a). Severely disabled visitors Fully exempt with a disability degree (GdB) of 100 (§ 5 (1) no. 5); from GdB 50 there is a 50 % reduction on presentation of the ID (§ 19 (1)). An accompanying person is free if mark B is entered (§ 5 (1) no. 6). Reduced beach cards are available at the beach-chair rentals and the spa administration. Pensioners No reduction – the by-law has no pensioner rate. Regular rates apply unless another exemption applies (e.g. Lübeck residence or severe disability). Students in Lübeck Exempt with a valid student ID of Lübeck’s universities (§ 5 (1) no. 3, § 14 e). Guests with guest cards of other SH resorts Exempt from the spa levy for one day if the resort is not part of the ostseecard network (§ 5 (2)); ostseecard holders from other resorts are free for the card’s validity (§ 5 (1) no. 8, § 14 c). Second-home owners Pay a flat annual spa levy of 98.00 € (28 days of the summer season, § 7 (2) and (3)); in certain cases 56.00 € on application.

abschnitte.s: Does the tax apply on the Priwall – and where is the beach free?
abschnitte.x: Yes – the Priwall is part of the levy area (§ 2 of the by-law). Fees apply to the managed Priwall beach between the Südermole and a line 120 m west of the state border with Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (§ 11), on the town side to the beach between Nordermole and the northern ramp, and to the lawn beach (Grünstrand). The nature beach below the Brodten cliff remains free of charge – walk there if you want to save.

abschnitte.s: Where and how do you pay – is online possible?
abschnitte.x: Overnight guests pay the spa levy via their host, who hands out the ostseecard; registration runs digitally via the online registration form (§ 9). Day visitors buy the beach card before entering at the machines at the beach entrances, from the beach-chair rentals – or digitally via app (§ 16; the spa administration names EasyPark). Note: paying only during an inspection incurs an additional administrative fee (§ 16 (4)); deliberate non-payment is an administrative offence with a fine of up to 2,500 € (§ 20).

abschnitte.s: What does the ostseecard give you?
abschnitte.x: The ostseecard is proof of the paid spa levy: it unlocks access to the managed beach sections and further spa services – the beach fee is already included for ostseecard holders (§ 14 c). Frequent visitors can buy the season beach card for 84.00 €, valid for the entire high season (§ 15, § 17). abschnitte.s: Visitor’s tax Travemünde at a glance
abschnitte.x: In Travemünde the Hansestadt Lübeck charges a spa levy from overnight guests (3.50 € per person per day in the high season from 15 May to 14 September, otherwise 2.00 €; the arrival day is not counted) and a beach fee from day visitors (3.50 €, 2.00 € after 3 p.m., high season only). Exempt are, among others, Lübeck residents, children and young people, severely disabled visitors with GdB 100 and students of Lübeck’s universities; from GdB 50 a 50 per cent reduction applies. Payment is made via the host, at beach machines or by app; the ostseecard serves as proof. The Priwall beach is subject to fees, the nature beach at the Brodten cliff is free. The legal basis is the Hansestadt Lübeck spa-levy by-law in the version effective from 15 May 2026.

abschnitte.s: What does the visitor’s tax cost in Travemünde in 2026?
abschnitte.x: Overnight guests pay 3.50 € per person per day in the high season (15 May to 14 September) and 2.00 € in the low season; the arrival day is not charged. Day visitors pay a 3.50 € beach fee in the high season, 2.00 € from 3 p.m. – outside the high season the beach is free.

abschnitte.s: Do Lübeck residents have to pay the visitor’s tax?
abschnitte.x: No. Anyone whose habitual or main residence is in the Hansestadt Lübeck is exempt from the spa levy (§ 5 (1) no. 7 of the by-law) and the beach fee (§ 14 d). Travemünde is a district of Lübeck – residents are not guests here.

abschnitte.s: Do pensioners pay less visitor’s tax?
abschnitte.x: No, the by-law has no pensioner rate – regular rates apply. Exemptions exist for other reasons, such as Lübeck residence or severe disability.

With a disability degree (GdB) of 100, yes (§ 5 (1) no. 5). From GdB 50 there is a 50 % reduction on presentation of the ID (§ 19 (1)). An accompanying person is exempt if mark B is entered (§ 5 (1) no. 6). More on this on the accessibility page.

abschnitte.s: From what age do you pay the visitor’s tax?
abschnitte.x: Overnight guests pay from 18 – children and young people are free up to the age of 18 (§ 5 (1) no. 1). The day-visitor beach fee applies from 16 (§ 14 a).

abschnitte.s: Does the tax apply on the Priwall?
abschnitte.x: Yes, the Priwall is part of the levy area (§ 2). Fees apply to the managed beach between the Südermole and 120 m before the state border with Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (§ 11 no. 2).

abschnitte.s: Where and how do you pay – also online?
abschnitte.x: Overnight guests pay via their host (digital online registration, § 9). Day visitors buy the beach card at the machines at the beach entrances, from the beach-chair rentals or digitally via app (§ 16); the spa administration names EasyPark.

abschnitte.s: Which beaches are free of the tax?
abschnitte.x: Fees apply only to the managed sections: town beach, Priwall beach and the lawn beach (§ 11). The nature beach below the Brodten cliff is free – and outside the high season no beach costs anything.

abschnitte.s: What happens if you don’t pay?
abschnitte.x: Paying the beach fee only during an inspection incurs an additional administrative fee (§ 16 (4)). Deliberate non-payment is an administrative offence with a fine of up to 2,500 € (§ 20).

abschnitte.s: What do you get for the visitor’s tax?
abschnitte.x: The ostseecard unlocks access to the managed beach sections and further spa services – the beach fee is included. It is also proof that the contribution has been paid.
Promenade circuit · around 2 hours · by ferry

Travemünde is best experienced on foot – flat, always by the water and with short distances. The centrepiece is the promenade circuit, which links the Travepromenade on the town side and the promenade on the Priwall via the two ferries into one loop. Add to that the path along the top of the cliff, the loop across the Priwall and the riverside path along the Trave. This page places the routes in context, with source and verification date.

The promenade circuit links the Travepromenade on the town side and the promenade on the Priwall into one loop – you cross the Trave with the passenger ferry at the Nordermole and the car ferry at the Vorderreihe. Start and finish is the Nordermole; allow around two hours for the full loop (without breaks). The path is flat and easy to walk.

abschnitte.t: Water level and high water in Travemünde
abschnitte.s: Why the Baltic Sea has hardly any tides
abschnitte.x: The Baltic Sea is nearly tide-free: the tidal range in the Bay of Lübeck is only a few centimetres – there is practically no ebb-and-flow rhythm as on the North Sea. Here the water level is mainly driven by the wind. Strong onshore wind from the north-east to east pushes water into the bay and raises the gauge – up to a storm surge. Offshore west to south-west wind pushes the water out, and the level falls (low water). The gauge is therefore not measured as “ebb/flow” but as a deviation from the mean water level – so high and low water can be read at a glance. What lies behind the missing ebb-and-flow rhythm is explained in detail on tides in the Baltic Sea .

abschnitte.t: Water level and high water in Travemünde
abschnitte.x: Storm surges are rare on the Baltic but possible – usually during sustained east/north-east storms in autumn and winter. The severe Baltic storm surge of 1872 is still regarded as a once-in-a-century event; a flood mark on the Old Lighthouse recalls it. During a warning, a banner appears at the top of this website (source: NINA/DWD); the official water-level forecast comes from the BSH. verified on 30 June 2026

abschnitte.t: Water level and high water in Travemünde
abschnitte.s: When does it count as a storm surge?
abschnitte.x: On the Baltic coast the Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH) classifies storm surges by the level above the German datum (NHN): from 1.00 metre above NHN a storm surge, from 1.25 metres a medium, from 1.50 metres a severe and from 2.00 metres a very severe storm surge. For the Travemünde gauge this means: the gauge datum lies 502 cm below NHN, so a storm surge here starts at 602 cm on the gauge. Unlike on the North Sea, the high water is driven not by the tide but by sustained wind – in north-easterly conditions it pushes water into the Bay of Lübeck. Official forecasts and warnings come from the BSH; the situation assessment above shows where Travemünde stands right now. abschnitte.s: What is normal over the year
abschnitte.x: In high summer (July/August) the Bay of Lübeck usually reaches 18 to 22 °C, occasionally more in warm spells. Spring is cool (May often 10–14 °C); in autumn the water holds its warmth longer than the air. In winter it drops towards freezing; iced-over bays are rare but possible.

On the Baltic, offshore wind turns the water over: with strong west/south-west wind the warm surface water is pushed away and colder water rises – the temperature can drop several degrees within a day. After calm sunny days it climbs back just as quickly.

Yes, Travemünde has wide free Wi-Fi: the official “GastWLAN” has been usable without a ticket since 2024 – from the promenade across the Kurstrand to the Priwall. The short answer: yes, Travemünde has wide free Wi-Fi. The resort operator’s official “GastWLAN” has been completely free to use since 2024 – no ticket, no Ostseecard, no registration. It covers the beach and Trave promenades, the Kurstrand, the Brügmanngarten, the tourist information and the old town – and across the Trave the Priwall promenade, Passat harbour and Priwall beach. For ferry travellers without a German data plan it is the most reliable connection in town; the best reception spots and further Wi-Fi places are in the overview below.

Dog beach year-round · main beach off-limits until 31 October

Dogs are welcome in Travemünde – with clear rules. At the designated dog-beach sections at the eastern Priwall and at the Brodten shore they can reach the water all year. On the main beach (Kurstrand) dogs are banned from 1 April to 31 October; from November to March they are allowed there too. This page gathers the beaches, the rules, travel with a dog and practical tips.

At the eastern end of the Priwall peninsula there is a designated dog-beach section – open to dogs all year, with plenty of space and quieter than the Kurstrand. Reach it via the Priwall ferry and then east along the beach; the naturist section is nearby (follow the signs).

North of the Kurstrand, below the Brodten cliffs towards Niendorf, there is another dog-beach section. A natural shore with stones rather than lawns – great for romping and long beach walks with a view of the cliffs.

abschnitte.s: Not allowed: main beach in season
abschnitte.x: The Kurstrand in front of the promenade is closed to dogs from 1 April to 31 October. In season, head to the Priwall east end or Brodten instead. Outside the season (1 November to 31 March) dogs are allowed on the main beach too. Proposed change As of July 2026: there is a political proposal (the “Bürger für Lübeck” group, backed by a petition with over 4,300 signatures) to allow dogs again from around 10 October – right after the kite festival. This has not been decided yet; the current rule (until 31 October) remains binding. abschnitte.s: Tips and tricks for a day with the dog
abschnitte.x: Bring fresh water and a bowl – salt water does not quench thirst and drinking points on the beach are scarce. Plan for shade: the open Baltic has little natural shade; a beach shelter or sun sail helps your dog. Watch for jellyfish in high summer – moon jellyfish are harmless, yellow-brown lion’s mane jellyfish can sting; avoid washed-up ones. Carry and use dog-waste bags – dispensers are not available at every access point. Come early or in the evening: on hot days the midday sand is hot and the beaches busy; mornings are cooler and quieter. For long walks, the Brodten cliffs are ideal – a firm path on top, natural shore below, for kilometres towards Niendorf. Leash etiquette: on the promenade, the Vorderreihe and the paths a leash is required; on the designated dog beach off-leash is usually allowed – the signs on site are binding. Dining with a dog: at Moin’sen im Fährhaus by the Priwall ferry landing, four-legged guests are expressly welcome.

abschnitte.s: Can the dog go on the beach in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: Yes, at the designated dog-beach sections at the eastern Priwall and at the Brodten shore, all year round. On the main beach (Kurstrand) dogs are banned from 1 April to 31 October; from November to March they are allowed there too.

abschnitte.s: Where is the dog beach in Travemünde?
abschnitte.x: There are two designated dog-beach sections: at the eastern end of the Priwall peninsula (reached via the Priwall ferry) and at the Brodten shore north of the Kurstrand. Both are open to dogs all year.

abschnitte.s: Do dogs have to be on a leash at the dog beach?
abschnitte.x: On the designated dog beach off-leash is usually allowed. On the promenade, the Vorderreihe and the access paths a leash is required. The signs on site are always decisive.

abschnitte.s: Can dogs use the main beach in summer?
abschnitte.x: No. The Kurstrand in front of the promenade bans dogs from 1 April to 31 October. During that time the Priwall east beach and the Brodten shore are the alternatives; from 1 November the main beach is open to dogs again.

abschnitte.s: Can I take a dog on the Priwall ferry or the train?
abschnitte.x: Leashed dogs are allowed on the Priwall ferry and on regional trains; larger dogs may need a ticket on the train. This makes the Priwall dog beach reachable without a car.

abschnitte.s: What to do in Travemünde with children when it rains?
abschnitte.x: The PriWilly Cosmos indoor play hall on the Priwall, the Ostseestation by the Trave, the Seebadmuseum – and the Passat can be visited in rain as well. The ferry ride across the Trave is a small adventure in itself.

abschnitte.s: Which playground is right on the beach?
abschnitte.x: The beach playground on the Kurstrand sits directly on the sand, within sight of the promenade. On the Priwall, the playground at the Priwallpromenade is similarly close to the water.

abschnitte.s: Is the climbing forest suitable for small children?
abschnitte.x: The climbing forest has courses at different heights; suitability depends on age and height – binding details are on the operator’s linked website.

abschnitte.s: Does the beach cost anything for families?
abschnitte.x: Travemünde charges a resort fee in season; current rates are listed on the official tourism site travemuende-tourismus.de.

abschnitte.s: Which day trips nearby are worth it with children?
abschnitte.x: Sea Life Timmendorfer Strand and the Vogelpark Niendorf are about 15 minutes away and good for a rainy day. Karls Erlebnis-Dorf in Warnsdorf (approx. 20 min) has free entry; Hansa-Park in Sierksdorf (approx. 25 min) is the region’s largest theme park. Opening hours and prices on the operators’ sites.

abschnitte.s: From what age is Travemünde suitable for children?
abschnitte.x: The gently sloping Kurstrand suits every age – toddlers paddle in the shallow water. From school age come the climbing forest (mind the minimum height), the laser maze at PriWilly Cosmos and boat trips on the Trave.

abschnitte.s: How do you get to Travemünde with children?
abschnitte.x: From Lübeck the train runs directly to Lübeck-Travemünde Strand; by car via the A1 and B75, parking near the beach. Details and live departures are on the getting-here page.
